Another reason to think about ethics in connection with law is that the laws themselves are meant to 
express some moral view. If there are legal prohibitions against cheating the Medicare program, it is 
because people (legislators or their agents) have collectively decided that cheating Medicare is wrong. If 
there are legal prohibitions against assisting someone to commit suicide, it is because there has been a 
group decision that doing so is immoral. Thus the law provides some important cues as to what society 
regards as right or wrong. 
Finally, important policy issues that face society are often resolved through law, but it is important to 
understand the moral perspectives that underlie public debate—as, for example, in the continuing 
controversies over stem-cell research, medical use of marijuana, and abortion. Some ethical perspectives 
focus on rights, some on social utility, some on virtue or character, and some on social justice. People 
consciously (or, more often, unconsciously) adopt one or more of these perspectives, and even if they 
completely agree on the facts with an opponent, they will not change their views. Fundamentally, the 
difference comes down to incompatible moral perspectives, a clash of basic values. These are hot-button 
issues because society is divided, not so much over facts, but over basic values. Understanding the varied 
moral perspectives and values in public policy debates is a clarifying benefit in following or participating 
in these important discussions.

qa_pairs.answer: It is important for a business to consider ethics in addition to law when making decisions because ethical considerations often reflect the moral values and societal norms that influence public perception and trust. While legal compliance is essential, ethical behavior can significantly impact a business's reputation, customer loyalty, and long-term success. Ethical practices can lead to a favorable view of the company, which is particularly valuable during the sale of a business, as goodwill is often counted as an asset. Conversely, legal troubles or a reputation for legal issues can diminish the value of a business and its stock. Moreover, laws themselves are a reflection of collective moral decisions, indicating what society deems right or wrong. Understanding the ethical perspectives underlying public policy debates, such as those on stem-cell research, medical marijuana, and abortion, is crucial for businesses to navigate societal divisions and align their practices with the values of their stakeholders. qa_pairs.question: How do ethical perspectives influence public policy debates and the resolution of important societal issues?
qa_pairs.answer: Ethical perspectives play a crucial role in shaping public policy debates and the resolution of important societal issues by providing the moral framework within which these discussions occur. Different ethical perspectives, such as those focusing on rights, social utility, virtue, character, and social justice, guide individuals and groups in their approach to policy-making. These perspectives often lead to divergent views on contentious issues, reflecting incompatible moral values and basic values. For instance, debates over stem-cell research, medical marijuana, and abortion are not solely about factual disagreements but are deeply rooted in differing ethical beliefs. Understanding these varied moral perspectives and values is essential for clarifying and participating in public policy debates. It allows individuals and businesses to appreciate the underlying values that drive public opinion and policy decisions, fostering a more informed and constructive dialogue. Recognizing the importance of ethical considerations in public policy helps society navigate complex issues and work towards resolutions that respect diverse moral viewpoints.

Some years ago, Royal Dutch/Shell (one of the world’s largest companies) found that it was in deep 
trouble with the public for its apparent carelessness with the environment and human rights. Consumers 
were boycotting and investors were getting frightened, so the company took a long, hard look at its ethic 
of short-term profit maximization. Since then, changes have been made. The CEO told one group of 
business ethicists that the uproar had taken them by surprise; they thought they had done everything 
right, but it seemed there was a “ghost in the machine.” That ghost was consumers, NGOs, and the media, 
all of whom objected to the company’s seeming lack of moral sensitivity. 
The market does respond to unethical behavior. In Section 2.4 "Corporations and Corporate Governance", 
you will read about the Sears Auto Centers case. The loss of goodwill toward Sears Auto Centers was real, 
even though the total amount of money lost cannot be clearly accounted for. Years later, there are people 
who will not go near a Sears Auto Center; the customers who lost trust in the company will never return, 
and many of their children may avoid Sears Auto Centers as well. 
 
The Arthur Andersen story is even more dramatic. A major accounting firm, Andersen worked closely 
with Enron in hiding its various losses through creative accounting measures. Suspiciously, Andersen’s 
Houston office also did some shredding around the clock, appearing to cover up what it was doing for 
Enron. A criminal case based on this shredding resulted in a conviction, later overturned by the Supreme 
Court. But it was too late. Even before the conviction, many clients had found other accounting firms that 
were not under suspicion, and the Supreme Court’s reversal came too late to save the company. Even 
without the conviction, Andersen would have lost significant market share.

Maximizing profits while being legally compliant is not a very inspiring goal for a business. People in an 
organization need some quality or excellence to strive for. By focusing on pushing the edge of what is 
legal, by looking for loopholes in the law that would help create short-term financial gain, companies have 
often learned that in the long term they are not actually satisfying the market, the shareholders, the 
suppliers, or the community generally. 
 
 
 
 
KEY TAKEAWAY 
 
Legal compliance is not the same as acting ethically. Your reputation, individually or corporately, depends on 
how others regard your actions. Goodwill is hard to measure or quantify, but it is real nonetheless and can 
best be protected by acting ethically.

qa_pairs.question: What was the irony of Andersen's situation despite its reputation for integrity and straightforward practices?
qa_pairs.answer: The irony of Andersen's situation, despite its reputation for integrity and straightforward practices, lies in the fact that the firm, which was founded on principles of honesty and straightforwardness, ultimately faced a downfall due to its involvement in overly aggressive accounting practices. Andersen's founder, who emphasized the motto 'Think straight, talk straight,' had built the company's reputation over a hundred years ago by refusing to engage in deceptive practices for potentially lucrative clients. However, the firm later found itself in a predicament where it had to push the boundaries of what was legal to maintain its market position. This focus on maximizing profits by exploiting legal loopholes led to a loss of trust and credibility, resulting in significant market share loss and the eventual reversal by the Supreme Court. The irony is that the firm, which prided itself on ethical practices, ended up compromising its integrity for short-term financial gain, ultimately leading to its downfall.

qa_pairs.question: Why is legal compliance not the same as acting ethically, and how does this distinction affect a company's reputation?
qa_pairs.answer: Legal compliance and ethical behavior, while related, are not the same. Legal compliance refers to adhering to laws and regulations, which are designed to maintain order and protect society. However, ethical behavior goes beyond legal requirements and encompasses a broader set of moral principles and values that guide how individuals and organizations conduct themselves. Acting ethically involves considering the impact of one's actions on others, including stakeholders, the community, and the environment, and striving to do what is right even when not explicitly required by law. This distinction is crucial for a company's reputation because it is built on the perception of its actions by others. Goodwill, which is the positive regard and trust that people have for a company, is difficult to measure but is a tangible asset that can be protected by acting ethically. When a company focuses solely on legal compliance without considering ethical implications, it risks damaging its reputation, losing the trust of its stakeholders, and ultimately failing to satisfy the market, shareholders, suppliers, and the community. Ethical behavior fosters a positive reputation, which can lead to long-term success and sustainability.

1. Describe the various major theories about ethics in human decision making. 
2. Begin considering how the major theories about ethics apply to difficult choices in life and business. 
 
 
There are several well-respected ways of looking at ethical issues. Some of them have been around for 
centuries. It is important to know that many who think a lot about business and ethics have deeply held 
beliefs about which perspective is best. Others would recommend considering ethical problems from a 
variety of different perspectives. Here, we take a brief look at (1) utilitarianism, (2) deontology, (3) social

such as general theories of justice and “rights” and feminist thought about ethics and patriarchy.

Utilitarianism is a prominent perspective on ethics, one that is well aligned with economics and the 
free-market outlook that has come to dominate much current thinking about business, management, and 
economics. Jeremy Bentham is often considered the founder of utilitarianism, though John Stuart Mill 
(who wrote On Liberty and Utilitarianism) and others promoted it as a guide to what is good. 
Utilitarianism emphasizes not rules but results. An action (or set of actions) is generally deemed good or 
right if it maximizes happiness or pleasure throughout society. Originally intended as a guide for 
legislators charged with seeking the greatest good for society, the utilitarian outlook may also be practiced 
individually and by corporations.

qa_pairs.question: What is the basic principle that forms the basis for your judgment that it was right?
qa_pairs.answer: The basic principle that forms the basis for my judgment that an action was right is the principle of utilitarianism. Utilitarianism is an ethical theory that suggests an action is right if it maximizes happiness or pleasure for the greatest number of people. This principle is rooted in the belief that the overall well-being of society is the ultimate measure of the morality of an action. In making a judgment, I would consider the consequences of the action and evaluate whether it leads to a net increase in happiness or pleasure for those affected. If the action results in a greater good for the majority, then it would be deemed right according to this principle.

qa_pairs.question: What is the basic principle that forms the basis for your judgment that it was wrong?
qa_pairs.answer: The basic principle that forms the basis for my judgment that an action was wrong is the principle of deontology. Deontology is an ethical theory that emphasizes the importance of following moral rules or duties, regardless of the consequences. According to this principle, an action is considered wrong if it violates a moral rule or duty, even if it leads to positive outcomes. In making a judgment, I would consider whether the action in question adheres to or violates a moral rule or duty. If the action violates a moral rule or duty, then it would be deemed wrong according to this principle.

Bentham believed that the most promising way to obtain agreement on the best policies for a society 
would be to look at the various policies a legislature could pass and compare the good and bad 
consequences of each. The right course of action from an ethical point of view would be to choose the 
policy that would produce the greatest amount of utility, or usefulness. In brief, the utilitarian principle 
holds that an action is right if and only if the sum of utilities produced by that action is greater than the 
sum of utilities from any other possible act. 
 
This statement describes “act utilitarianism”—which action among various options will deliver the 
greatest good to society? “Rule utilitarianism” is a slightly different version; it asks, what rule or principle, 
if followed regularly, will create the greatest good? 
 
Notice that the emphasis is on finding the best possible results and that the assumption is that we can 
measure the utilities involved. (This turns out to be more difficult that you might think.) Notice also that 
“the sum total of utilities” clearly implies that in doing utilitarian analysis, we cannot be satisfied if an act 
or set of acts provides the greatest utility to us as individuals or to a particular corporation; the test is, 
instead, whether it provides the greatest utility to society as a whole. Notice that the theory does not tell us 
what kinds of utilities may be better than others or how much better a good today is compared with a 
good a year from today.

qa_pairs.question: What is the primary focus of utilitarian thinking in the context of US law and business?
qa_pairs.answer: The primary focus of utilitarian thinking in the context of US law and business is to achieve the greatest good for society as a whole. This approach is evident in various applications such as cost-benefit analysis in administrative and regulatory rules, environmental impact studies, majority voting, product comparisons for consumer information, marketing studies, tax laws, and strategic planning. Utilitarianism emphasizes finding the best possible results and assumes that utilities can be measured. It requires that actions or policies be evaluated based on whether they provide the greatest utility to society, rather than just to individuals or corporations. This principle is applied in diverse areas, aiming to maximize overall societal benefits rather than focusing solely on the interests of specific entities.

qa_pairs.question: How does act utilitarianism differ from rule utilitarianism?
qa_pairs.answer: Act utilitarianism and rule utilitarianism are two different approaches within utilitarian thinking. Act utilitarianism focuses on evaluating individual actions to determine which one will deliver the greatest good to society. It asks, 'What action among various options will produce the greatest good?' On the other hand, rule utilitarianism considers the long-term effects of following certain rules or principles consistently. It asks, 'What rule or principle, if followed regularly, will create the greatest good?' While act utilitarianism assesses the consequences of specific actions, rule utilitarianism emphasizes the importance of adhering to rules that, when followed by everyone, lead to the best overall outcomes for society. Both approaches aim to maximize utility, but they differ in their focus on individual actions versus general rules.

An individual or a company that consistently uses the test “What’s the greatest good for me or the

see only one or two options that seem reasonable. The following are some frequent mistakes that people 
make in applying what they think are utilitarian principles in justifying their chosen course of action: 
 
1. Failing to come up with lots of options that seem reasonable and then choosing the one that has the 
greatest benefit for the greatest number. Often, a decision maker seizes on one or two alternatives 
without thinking carefully about other courses of action. If the alternative does more good than 
harm, the decision maker assumes it’s ethically okay. 
2. Assuming that the greatest good for you or your company is in fact the greatest good for all—that is, 
looking at situations subjectively or with your own interests primarily in mind. 
3. Underestimating the costs of a certain decision to you or your company. The now-classic Ford Pinto 
case demonstrates how Ford Motor Company executives drastically underestimated the legal costs 
of not correcting a feature on their Pinto models that they knew could cause death or injury. 
General Motors was often taken to task by juries that came to understand that the company would 
not recall or repair known and dangerous defects because it seemed more profitable not to. In 
2010, Toyota learned the same lesson. 
4. Underestimating the cost or harm of a certain decision to someone else or some other group of 
people. 
5. Favoring short-term benefits, even though the long-term costs are greater.

qa_pairs.question: What are some common mistakes people make when applying utilitarian principles in justifying their chosen course of action?
qa_pairs.answer: Common mistakes in applying utilitarian principles include failing to generate a wide range of reasonable options before choosing the one that benefits the greatest number, assuming that one's own or a company's greatest good is the same as the greatest good for all, underestimating the costs of a decision to oneself or one's company, underestimating the cost or harm of a decision to others, favoring short-term benefits over long-term costs, and assuming that all values can be reduced to money. qa_pairs.question: How does the deontological view presented in the writings of Immanuel Kant differ from the utilitarian perspective?
qa_pairs.answer: The deontological view, as presented by Immanuel Kant, differs from the utilitarian perspective in that it emphasizes the importance of having a moral intent and following the right rules as a path to ethical conduct, rather than focusing solely on the outcomes or consequences of actions. Kantian ethics, or deontology, posits that certain actions are inherently right or wrong, regardless of their consequences. This contrasts with the utilitarian approach, which evaluates the morality of actions based on their ability to produce the greatest good for the greatest number. Kant's philosophy suggests that ethical behavior is determined by adherence to moral duties and principles, rather than by the pursuit of the greatest overall benefit.

The second requirement for an action to be universal is the search for consistency. This is more abstract. 
A deontologist would say that since you know you are telling a lie, you must be willing to say that lying, as 
a general, universal phenomenon, is acceptable. But if everyone lied, then there would be no point to 
lying, since no one would believe anyone. It is only because honesty works well for society as a whole and 
is generally practiced that lying even becomes possible! That is, lying cannot be universalized, for it 
depends on the preexistence of honesty. 
 
Similar demonstrations can be made for actions such as polluting, breaking promises, and committing 
most crimes, including rape, murder, and theft. But these are the easy cases for Kantian thinkers. In the 
gray areas of life as it is lived, the consistency test is often difficult to apply. If breaking a promise would 
save a life, then Kantian thought becomes difficult to apply. If some amount of pollution can allow 
employment and the harm is minimal or distant, Kantian thinking is not all that helpful. Finally, we 
should note that the well-known Golden Rule, “Do unto others as you would have them do unto you,” 
emphasizes the easier of the two universalizing requirements: practicing reversibility (“How would I like it 
if someone did this to me?”).

This involves considering whether one would be willing to accept the action as a general, universal phenomenon. qa_pairs.question: How do social justice theorists approach the concept of distributive justice, and what are the contrasting views of Marxist and capitalist thought on this matter?
qa_pairs.answer: Social justice theorists are concerned with distributive justice, which involves determining the fair way to distribute goods among a group of people. Marxist thought advocates for the distribution of goods according to people's needs, which would necessitate a governing power to make decisions about who receives what and when. On the other hand, capitalist thought rejects any form of giving that is not voluntary, emphasizing that goods should be distributed based on voluntary exchanges. This approach contrasts with Marxist thought, which supports a more structured redistribution of resources to meet individual needs. The debate between these two perspectives highlights the complexities of achieving distributive justice and the different philosophical foundations that underpin each approach.

qa_pairs.question: What is the social contract theory and how does it relate to the existence of corporations and government?
qa_pairs.answer: The social contract theory, as proposed by Thomas Hobbes, suggests that individuals in a 'state of nature' would rationally choose to establish some form of government in exchange for security and common benefits. This theory implies that people give up certain rights to the government for the greater good. In the context of corporations, some commentators argue that there is a social contract between corporations and society. This ongoing balancing act between human desires for freedom and human desires for order is an ancient tension. The social contract theory can also be applied to various communities, not just nations, which make rules for the common good. qa_pairs.question: What are the views of capitalist economists like Milton Friedman on the role of corporations in society?
qa_pairs.answer: Capitalist economists like Milton Friedman believe that corporations should not have a duty to give to unmet needs in society. They argue that any giving should be voluntary and that the government should play the role of addressing societal needs. According to Friedman, the government's role should include providing certain forms of welfare, such as Social Security, Medicare, assistance to flood-stricken areas, and help for AIDS patients. He also acknowledges the need for some government and public goods, such as defense, education, highways, parks, and support of key industries affecting national security. However, he rejects the notion that corporations have a duty to give to unmet needs in society. Even the most dedicated free-market capitalist would often admit the need for some government and some forms of welfare, but they believe that the government should play that role, not corporations.

qa_pairs.question: How does the communitarian outlook differ from deontological and natural-law perspectives in terms of the origin of rights?
qa_pairs.answer: The communitarian outlook differs significantly from deontological and natural-law perspectives regarding the origin of rights. Communitarians emphasize that rights are inherently connected to corresponding duties, meaning that there cannot be a right without a corresponding duty. This perspective contrasts with deontological and natural-law thinkers, such as Gandhi, Jesus, and Martin Luther King Jr., who believe that rights originate from a transcendent moral order or God. Communitarians argue that rights are derived from the social contract within a society, which is shaped by the collective agreements and interactions of its members. This view suggests that rights are not absolute or universal but are instead contingent upon the specific social and cultural context in which they are established. Communitarians, therefore, focus on the responsibilities and obligations that come with rights, advocating for a balance between individual freedoms and the collective good.

qa_pairs.question: What is the relationship between rights and duties according to the text, and how does it apply to free expression and physical assault?
qa_pairs.answer: The text explains that rights inherently come with corresponding duties, meaning there cannot be a right without a duty. qa_pairs.question: How does the text distinguish between basic rights and nonbasic rights, and what are some examples of positive and negative rights?
qa_pairs.answer: The text distinguishes between basic rights and nonbasic rights by categorizing basic rights as fundamental elements necessary for survival and well-being, such as food, water, shelter, and physical safety. Nonbasic rights, on the other hand, are not essential for survival but are still important for a functioning society. The text also differentiates between positive rights, which are entitlements to certain benefits or services provided by the state, such as the right to bear arms, the right to vote, and the right to privacy. Negative rights, in contrast, are freedoms from certain actions by the state or others, such as the right to be free from unreasonable searches and seizures and the right to be free from cruel or unusual punishments. Aristotle and Virtue Theory 
Virtue theory, or virtue ethics, has received increasing attention over the past twenty years, particularly 
in contrast to utilitarian and deontological approaches to ethics. Virtue theory emphasizes the value of 
virtuous qualities rather than formal rules or useful results. Aristotle is often recognized as the first 
philosopher to advocate the ethical value of certain qualities, or virtues, in a person’s character. As LaRue 
Hosmer has noted, Aristotle saw the goal of human existence as the active, rational search for excellence, 
and excellence requires the personal virtues of honesty, truthfulness, courage, temperance, generosity, 
and high-mindedness. This pursuit is also termed “knowledge of the good” in Greek philosophy. [1] 
 
Aristotle believed that all activity was aimed at some goal or perceived good and that there must be some

qa_pairs.question: How does Michael Josephson's Core Values Analysis and Decision Process help in identifying ethical qualities in individuals and corporations?
qa_pairs.answer: Michael Josephson's Core Values Analysis and Decision Process provides a framework for identifying and applying ethical qualities in both personal and corporate decisions. qa_pairs.question: What are the three issues that emerge when considering the relevance of virtues in modern society and their application to corporations?

Second, there is the debate on the usefulness of having a list of agreed-upon virtues, as it may be challenging to establish a universally accepted set of virtues in a diverse and rapidly changing society. Third, there is the question of how virtues relate to corporations, particularly large ones where various groups and individuals may have little or no contact with other parts of the organization. If a company solely focuses on the bottom line, other values may diminish or disappear. Many books have been written in the past twenty years emphasizing the need for businesses to define their values to remain competitive in today's global economy. By addressing these issues, we can better understand the role of virtues in shaping ethical and value-driven practices in both individuals and corporations.

Trustworthiness involves being honest and keeping promises, while respect entails treating others with consideration and valuing their rights. Responsibility refers to being accountable for one's actions and fulfilling one's duties. Fairness is about treating others justly and without favoritism. qa_pairs.question: How do the six core values identified by the Josephson Institute of Ethics relate to other ethical values that may not be universally agreed upon?
qa_pairs.answer: The six core values identified by the Josephson Institute of Ethics—trustworthiness, respect, responsibility, fairness, caring, and citizenship—share a commonality with other ethical values that may not be universally agreed upon, such as thrift, temperance, and sexual abstinence. While these six core values are widely accepted and practiced by most people, other ethical values can vary significantly based on individual beliefs, cultural norms, and personal choices. For instance, some families and individuals may strongly believe in the virtue of saving money or abstaining from alcohol or sex prior to marriage, while others may not share these beliefs or practices. Despite these differences, it is possible to uphold the six core values even if one engages in behaviors that are not universally endorsed, such as taking on heavy debt, drinking heavily, or having frequent premarital sex. The key distinction is that the six core values have a higher degree of unanimity in their approval and practice, making them more universally recognized as ethical traits compared to other values that may be subject to greater disagreement and variation.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE 
 
1. Understand one model for ethical decision making: a process to arrive at the most ethical option for an 
individual or a business organization, using a virtue ethics approach combined with some elements of 
stakeholder analysis and utilitarianism. 
 
 
Josephson’s Core Values Model 
Once you recognize that there is a decision that involves ethical judgment, Michael Josephson would first 
have you ask as many questions as are necessary to get a full background on the relevant facts. Then, 
assuming you have all the needed information, the decision process is as follows: 
1. Identify the stakeholders. That is, who are the potential gainers and losers in the various decisions 
that might be made here? 
2. Identify several likely or reasonable decisions that could be made. 
3. Consider which stakeholders gain or lose with each decision. 
4. Determine which decision satisfies the greatest number of core values. 
5. If there is no decision that satisfies the greatest number of core values, try to determine which 
decision delivers the greatest good to the various stakeholders. 
 
It is often helpful to identify who (or what group) is the most important stakeholder, and why. In Milton 
Friedman’s view, it will always be the shareholders. In the view of John Mackey, the CEO of Whole Foods 
Market, the long-term viability and profitability of the organization may require that customers come 
first, or, at times, some other stakeholder group (see “Conscious Capitalism” in Section 2.4 "Corporations 
and Corporate Governance").

Shareholders and Stakeholders 
There are two main views about what the corporation’s duties are. The first view—maximizing profits—is 
the prevailing view among business managers and in business schools. This view largely follows the idea 
of Milton Friedman that the duty of a manager is to maximize return on investment to the owners. In 
essence, managers’ legally prescribed duties are those that make their employment possible. In terms of 
the legal organization of the corporation, the shareholders elect directors who hire managers, who have 
legally prescribed duties toward both directors and shareholders. Those legally prescribed duties are a 
reflection of the fact that managers are managing other people’s money and have a moral duty to act as a 
responsible agent for the owners. In law, this is called the manager’s fiduciary duty. Directors have the 
same duties toward shareholders. Friedman emphasized the primacy of this duty in his writings about 
corporations and social responsibility. 
 
Maximizing Profits: Milton Friedman 
Economist Milton Friedman is often quoted as having said that the only moral duty a corporation has is to 
make the most possible money, or to maximize profits, for its stockholders. Friedman’s beliefs are noted 
at length (see sidebar on Friedman’s article from the New York Times), but he asserted in a now-famous 
1970 article that in a free society, “there is one and only one social responsibility of business: to use its 
resources and engage in activities designed to increase its profits as long as it stays within the rules of the 
game, which is to say, engages in open and free competition without deception and fraud.” What follows is 
a major portion of what Friedman had to say in 1970.

Stakeholder Theory 
Stakeholders of a corporation include its employees, suppliers, customers, and the community. 
Stakeholder is a deliberate play on the word shareholder, to emphasize that corporations have obligations

qa_pairs.question: What is the primary argument against corporate executives spending money on reducing pollution beyond what is legally required or in the best interests of the corporation?
qa_pairs.answer: The primary argument against corporate executives spending money on reducing pollution beyond what is legally required or in the best interests of the corporation is that such expenditures are essentially spending someone else's money for a general social interest. This can reduce returns to stockholders, raise prices for customers, and lower wages for employees, all of which are seen as spending the money of others. The argument posits that corporate executives should focus on maximizing profits and fulfilling their obligations to shareholders, rather than diverting resources to broader social objectives that may not align with the corporation's best interests.

qa_pairs.question: How does Stakeholder Theory differ from traditional shareholder theory in terms of corporate responsibilities?
qa_pairs.answer: Stakeholder Theory differs from traditional shareholder theory by expanding the range of individuals and institutions to which a corporation owes moral consideration. While shareholder theory focuses on maximizing profits for shareholders, Stakeholder Theory argues that corporations have responsibilities toward a broader group of stakeholders, including employees, suppliers, customers, and the community. Stakeholders are defined as anyone significantly affected by the decisions of another moral agent, either positively or negatively. This theory emphasizes that corporations, as creations of law, have obligations that extend beyond profit maximization to include the well-being of all stakeholders, reflecting a more inclusive approach to corporate governance and ethical responsibility.

qa_pairs.question: What is the key concept for corporations that allows shareholders to only lose their investments in case of failure, without risking personal assets?
qa_pairs.answer: The key concept for corporations that allows shareholders to only lose their investments in case of failure, without risking personal assets, is limited liability. Limited liability means that shareholders are not personally responsible for the debts and obligations of the corporation beyond the amount they have invested in the company. This legal protection encourages investment and risk-taking, as shareholders can participate in larger enterprises without the fear of losing personal assets other than the value of their corporate stock. Limited liability is a fundamental principle that underpins the corporate form, enabling the aggregation of larger pools of capital for more significant ventures.

qa_pairs.question: How did New Jersey and Delaware change their laws in the late 1800s to make incorporating easier, and what is the implicit social contract between governments and corporations?
qa_pairs.answer: In the late 1800s, New Jersey and Delaware changed their laws to make incorporating easier by allowing incorporation for any legal purpose, rather than requiring a demonstration of a public purpose. This shift made it more straightforward for individuals and entities to form corporations, as they no longer needed to go to legislatures to show a public benefit. The implicit social contract between governments and corporations is that as long as corporations are considered socially useful, they can exist. Governments grant limited liability to corporations through charters, recognizing the benefits of encouraging capital and innovation. In return, corporations are expected to operate within the law and contribute positively to society. This social contract implies that corporations have a duty to be socially responsible, not just to their shareholders but also to other stakeholders affected by their decisions.

Ethical Leadership Is Top-Down 
People in an organization tend to watch closely what the top managers do and say. Regardless of 
managers’ talk about ethics, employees quickly learn what speech or actions are in fact rewarded. If the 
CEO is firm about acting ethically, others in the organization will take their cues from him or her. People 
at the top tend to set the target, the climate, the beliefs, and the expectations that fuel behavior. 
Accountability Is Often Weak 
Clever managers can learn to shift blame to others, take credit for others’ work, and move on before 
“funny numbers” or other earnings management tricks come to light. [1] Again, we see that the manager is 
often an agent for himself or herself and will often act more in his or her self-interest than for the 
corporate interest. 
 
Killing the Messenger 
Where organizations no longer function, inevitably some employees are unhappy. If they call attention to 
problems that are being covered up by coworkers or supervisors, they bring bad news. Managers like to 
hear good news and discourage bad news. Intentionally or not, those who told on others, or blew the 
whistle, have rocked the boat and become unpopular with those whose defalcations they report on and 
with the managers who don’t really want to hear the bad news. In many organizations, “killing the 
messenger” solves the problem. Consider James Alexander at Enron Corporation, who was deliberately 
shut out after bringing problems to CEO Ken Lay’s attention. [2]When Sherron Watkins sent Ken Lay a 
letter warning him about Enron’s accounting practices, CFO Andrew Fastow tried to fire her. [3] 
 
Ethics Codes 
Without strong leadership and a willingness to listen to bad news as well as good news, managers do not 
have the feedback necessary to keep the organization healthy. Ethics codes have been put in place—partly 
in response to federal sentencing guidelines and partly to encourage feedback loops to top management. 
The best ethics codes are aspirational, or having an ideal to be pursued, not legalistic or compliance 
driven. The Johnson & Johnson ethics code predated the Tylenol scare and the company’s oft-celebrated 
corporate response. [4] The corporate response was consistent with that code, which was lived and 
modeled by the top of the organization.

qa_pairs.question: How does the behavior of top managers influence the ethical climate within an organization?
qa_pairs.answer: The behavior of top managers significantly influences the ethical climate within an organization. Employees closely observe and emulate the actions and words of their leaders, particularly those at the top. If the CEO and other senior managers consistently demonstrate ethical behavior, it sets a positive example for the rest of the organization. This top-down approach helps establish the target, climate, beliefs, and expectations that drive behavior throughout the company. Conversely, if top managers engage in unethical practices, such as shifting blame, taking credit for others' work, or ignoring earnings management tricks, it sends a message that unethical behavior is acceptable. This can lead to a culture where unethical actions are normalized and even rewarded, undermining the organization's integrity and ethical standards.

qa_pairs.question: Why are ethics codes important in organizations, and what makes them effective?
qa_pairs.answer: Ethics codes are crucial in organizations as they provide a framework for expected behavior and help establish a culture of integrity. They are important because they offer guidance on ethical conduct, helping employees navigate complex situations and make decisions that align with the organization's values. Effective ethics codes are aspirational, setting an ideal to be pursued rather than merely complying with legal requirements. They encourage feedback loops to top management, ensuring that leaders are aware of both positive and negative aspects of the organization's operations. The Johnson & Johnson ethics code, for example, predated the Tylenol scare and was instrumental in the company's response, demonstrating the importance of having a strong, lived, and modeled code of ethics by top management. Ultimately, the effectiveness of an ethics code depends on the commitment of top management to uphold and model the principles outlined in the code, making it a living document that guides the organization's actions and decisions.

qa_pairs.question: What is the significance of having an ongoing process to root out wrongdoing at all levels of a company in the context of legal fines?
qa_pairs.answer: Having an ongoing process to root out wrongdoing at all levels of a company is considered a major mitigating factor when a judge is determining the fines a company will pay for legal and ethical violations. This is because it demonstrates the company's commitment to ethical behavior and its proactive efforts to prevent misconduct. Most Fortune 500 companies have established ethics hotlines and processes to identify and address legal and ethical problems within the organization. By showing that the company has taken steps to prevent wrongdoing, it can potentially reduce the severity of the penalties imposed by the court.

qa_pairs.question: How did the belief that 'stock price is all that matters' influence corporate behavior and ethical judgments according to Jeffrey Pfeffer?
qa_pairs.answer: Jeffrey Pfeffer, a professor of organizational behavior at Stanford University, argues that the belief that 'stock price is all that matters' has been deeply ingrained in the corporate psyche. This belief influences not only how individuals and companies assess their worth but also how they perceive their own roles and the work they do. Over time, this focus on stock prices has obscured ethical judgments, leading to a culture where winning, often measured by financial performance, is prioritized above all else. This has resulted in a tendency to lie about financial numbers and engage in questionable practices to achieve higher stock prices, as seen in the case of Enron, where the mantra of '15 percent a year or better earnings growth' became a driving force behind unethical behavior.

qa_pairs.question: What is the 'us versus them' mentality mentioned in the Sears case, and how does it relate to Kantian terms?
qa_pairs.answer: The 'us versus them' mentality in the Sears case refers to the division between Sears 'insiders' and customers, who were treated as 'outsiders.' This mentality aligns with Kantian terms, where outsiders were used merely as means to the benefit of insiders, rather than being treated as ends in themselves. In Kantian ethics, individuals should be treated with dignity and respect, recognizing their intrinsic value. However, Sears' approach effectively disregarded the customers' value, prioritizing the interests of insiders over the well-being of the customers.

qa_pairs.question: How does the conscious capitalism movement aim to integrate stakeholder theory and shareholder primacy?
qa_pairs.answer: The conscious capitalism movement seeks to integrate stakeholder theory and shareholder primacy by promoting a holistic or systems view that recognizes the interdependence of all stakeholders. Companies practicing conscious capitalism strive for win-win-win outcomes, where profits and prosperity coexist with social justice and environmental stewardship. They reject the notion of false trade-offs between stakeholder interests and aim to achieve a balance that benefits all parties involved. By focusing on a higher purpose beyond merely maximizing profits, conscious businesses aim to create a sustainable and ethical business model that aligns with the principles of conscious capitalism.

Conscious business leaders serve as such stewards, focusing on fulfilling the company’s purpose, 
delivering value to its stakeholders, and facilitating a harmony of interests, rather than on personal gain 
and self-aggrandizement. Why is this refocusing needed? Within the standard profit-maximizing model, 
corporations have long had to deal with the “agency problem.” Actions by top-level managers—acting on 
behalf of the company—should align with the shareholders, but in a culture all about winning and money, 
managers sometimes act in ways that are self-aggrandizing and that do not serve the interests of 
shareholders. Laws exist to limit such self-aggrandizing, but the remedies are often too little and too late 
and often catch only the most egregious overreaching. Having a culture of servant leadership is a much 
better way to see that a company’s top management works to ensure a harmony of interests.

Summary 
Doing good business requires attention to ethics as well as law. Understanding the long-standing 
perspectives on ethics—utilitarianism, deontology, social contract, and virtue ethics—is helpful in sorting 
out the ethical issues that face us as individuals and businesses. Each business needs to create or maintain 
a culture of ethical excellence, where there is ongoing dialogue not only about the best technical practices 
but also about the company’s ethical challenges and practices. A firm that has purpose and passion 
beyond profitability is best poised to meet the needs of diverse stakeholders and can best position itself 
for long-term, sustainable success for shareholders and other stakeholders as well.

qa_pairs.question: What does Friedman mean by 'ethical custom' in the context of business practices?
qa_pairs.answer: In the context of business practices, Milton Friedman refers to 'ethical custom' as the set of moral principles and standards that guide the behavior of individuals and organizations within a society. These customs are not necessarily codified into law but are widely accepted and followed by the community. They represent the collective conscience of society and serve as a benchmark for what is considered right or wrong in business dealings. According to Friedman, businesses have a responsibility to adhere to these ethical customs, as they are essential for maintaining trust and integrity in the marketplace. By following ethical customs, businesses contribute to the overall well-being of society and ensure that their operations are not only legally compliant but also morally sound.

qa_pairs.question: Should a company limit its profits if the law is 'on the books' but not enforced, and what are the ethical implications of such actions?
qa_pairs.answer: When a company considers limiting its profits due to a law that is 'on the books' but not actively enforced, it faces a complex ethical dilemma. On one hand, the company may argue that it is operating within the legal framework, as the law is technically in place. However, the lack of enforcement raises questions about the company's commitment to ethical practices and social responsibility. Ethically, the company should consider the broader impact of its actions on the community, environment, and stakeholders. Discharging pollutants into a river, for example, may save money in the short term but can have detrimental effects on the ecosystem and public health. Even if other companies in the industry are engaging in similar practices, it does not justify unethical behavior. The company should strive to go beyond mere legal compliance and adopt a proactive approach to ethical decision-making, considering the long-term consequences of its actions and the potential harm to society and the environment. By doing so, the company can contribute to a culture of ethical excellence and sustainable success.

law. Today, much of the law comes from Congress and the state legislatures. But it is in the courts

Robinson v. Audi 
Harry and Kay Robinson purchased a new Audi automobile from Seaway Volkswagen, Inc. (Seaway), in 
Massena, New York, in 1976. The following year the Robinson family, who resided in New York, left that

rear, causing a fire that severely burned Kay Robinson and her two children. Later on, the Robinsons 
brought a products-liability action in the District Court for Creek County, Oklahoma, claiming that their 
injuries resulted from the defective design and placement of the Audi’s gas tank and fuel system. They 
sued numerous defendants, including the automobile’s manufacturer, Audi NSU Auto Union 
Aktiengesellschaft (Audi); its importer, Volkswagen of America, Inc. (Volkswagen); its regional 
distributor, World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. (World-Wide); and its retail dealer, Seaway.

If the Robinsons choose to file their action in state court, they will need to consider the jurisdictional requirements of the state court. If they choose to file their action in federal court, they will need to consider the jurisdictional requirements of the federal court. In either case, the Robinsons will need to consider the laws and regulations that apply to their case, including the laws and regulations related to products liability, personal injury, and consumer protection.

qa_pairs.question: What are the two alternatives to litigation that the Robinsons could consider, and how do they differ from traditional court proceedings?
qa_pairs.answer: The Robinsons could consider mediation and arbitration as alternatives to litigation. Mediation is a process in which a neutral third party, called a mediator, helps the disputing parties to reach a mutually acceptable resolution. The mediator does not make a decision for the parties, but rather facilitates communication and negotiation between them. Mediation is often less formal, less time-consuming, and less expensive than traditional court proceedings. Arbitration, on the other hand, is a process in which a neutral third party, called an arbitrator, hears the evidence and arguments presented by the parties and then makes a binding decision. Arbitration is often used in commercial disputes and is similar to traditional court proceedings in that it involves the presentation of evidence and arguments, but it is generally less formal and less time-consuming. Both mediation and arbitration can be used to resolve disputes without going to court, and they can be less adversarial and more collaborative than traditional court proceedings.

in the United States 
 
LEARNING OBJECTIVES 
 
1. Understand the different but complementary roles of state and federal court systems. 
2. Explain why it makes sense for some courts to hear and decide only certain kinds of cases. 
3. Describe the difference between a trial court and an appellate court. 
 
 
Although it is sometimes said that there are two separate court systems, the reality is more complex. 
There are, in fact, fifty-two court systems: those of the fifty states, the local court system in the 
District of Columbia, and the federal court system. At the same time, these are not entirely separate; 
they all have several points of contact. 
 
State and local courts must honor both federal law and the laws of the other states. First, state courts 
must honor federal law where state laws are in conflict with federal laws (under the supremacy 
clause of the Constitution; see Chapter 4 "Constitutional Law and US Commerce"). Second, claims 
arising under federal statutes can often be tried in the state courts, where the Constitution or 
Congress has not explicitly required that only federal courts can hear that kind of claim. Third, under 
the full faith and credit clause, each state court is obligated to respect the final judgments of courts in 
other states. Thus a contract dispute resolved by an Arkansas court cannot be relitigated in North 
Dakota when the plaintiff wants to collect on the Arkansas judgment in North Dakota. Fourth, state

states have an interest, such as when drivers from two different states collide in a third state. Under 
these circumstances, state judges will consult their own state’s case decisions involving conflicts of 
laws and sometimes decide that they must apply another state’s laws to decide the case (see Table 3.1 
"Sample Conflict-of-Law Principles"). 
 
As state courts are concerned with federal law, so federal courts are often concerned with state law 
and with what happens in state courts. Federal courts will consider state-law-based claims when a

qa_pairs.question: What are the different roles of state and federal court systems in the United States, and why is it beneficial for some courts to handle only specific types of cases?
qa_pairs.answer: In the United States, the state and federal court systems play complementary roles, each with its own jurisdiction and responsibilities. State courts are primarily responsible for interpreting and applying state laws, while federal courts handle cases involving federal laws, the U.S. Constitution, and disputes between states or between a state and the federal government. The distinction between state and federal courts is not absolute; they intersect in various ways. State courts must respect federal law, especially when state laws conflict with federal laws, as mandated by the supremacy clause of the Constitution. Additionally, state courts can hear claims arising under federal statutes unless Congress explicitly requires federal courts to handle them. The full faith and credit clause obligates state courts to respect the final judgments of courts in other states, ensuring consistency and legal certainty across state lines. State courts also consider the laws of other states in cases involving conflicts of laws, such as interstate accidents. Federal courts, on the other hand, often deal with state-law-based claims when a federal question is involved. This division of responsibilities allows for specialized and efficient adjudication of cases, ensuring that each court system can focus on its respective areas of expertise.

qa_pairs.question: How do state courts handle cases involving conflicts of laws, and what principles do they use to decide which state's laws to apply?
qa_pairs.answer: State courts handle cases involving conflicts of laws by considering the laws of other states when deciding cases where two states have an interest. This often occurs in situations such as interstate accidents or disputes involving parties from different states. To determine which state's laws to apply, state courts use conflict-of-law principles, which are legal doctrines that guide the selection of the appropriate jurisdiction's laws. These principles take into account factors such as the location of the parties, the place where the relevant events occurred, and the interests of the states involved. State courts may consult their own state's case decisions involving conflicts of laws and sometimes decide that they must apply another state's laws to resolve the case. This approach ensures that the most relevant and appropriate laws are applied, promoting fairness and consistency in the resolution of interstate disputes.

Constitution—the concern that judges in one state court would favor the in-state plaintiff rather than 
a nonresident defendant. Another reason there are so many diversity cases is that plaintiffs’ 
attorneys know that removal is common and that it will move the case along faster by filing in federal 
court to begin with. Some plaintiffs’ attorneys also find advantages in pursuing a lawsuit in federal 
court. Federal court procedures are often more efficient than state court procedures, so that federal 
dockets are often less crowded. This means a case will get to trial faster, and many lawyers enjoy the 
higher status that comes in practicing before the federal bench. In some federal districts, judgments 
for plaintiffs may be higher, on average, than in the local state court. In short, not only law but also 
legal strategy factor into the popularity of diversity cases in federal courts. 
 
 
State Court Systems 
The vast majority of civil lawsuits in the United States are filed in state courts. Two aspects of civil 
lawsuits are common to all state courts: trials and appeals. A court exercising a trial function 
has original jurisdiction—that is, jurisdiction to determine the facts of the case and apply the law to 
them. A court that hears appeals from the trial court is said to have appellate jurisdiction—it must 
accept the facts as determined by the trial court and limit its review to the lower court’s theory of the 
applicable law. 
 
Limited Jurisdiction Courts 
In most large urban states and many smaller states, there are four and sometimes five levels of courts. The 
lowest level is that of the limited jurisdiction courts. These are usually county or municipal courts with 
original jurisdiction to hear minor criminal cases (petty assaults, traffic offenses, and breach of peace, 
among others) and civil cases involving monetary amounts up to a fixed ceiling (no more than $10,000 in 
most states and far less in many states). Most disputes that wind up in court are handled in the 18,000-
plus limited jurisdiction courts, which are estimated to hear more than 80 percent of all cases.

qa_pairs.question: What is the original jurisdiction of limited jurisdiction courts in the United States?
qa_pairs.answer: Limited jurisdiction courts in the United States, which are typically county or municipal courts, have original jurisdiction to hear minor criminal cases and civil cases involving monetary amounts up to a fixed ceiling. This ceiling is generally no more than $10,000 in most states, although it is often lower in many states. These courts handle a significant portion of legal disputes, with an estimated 80 percent of all cases being heard in the 18,000-plus limited jurisdiction courts across the country.

qa_pairs.question: Why might plaintiffs' attorneys prefer to file lawsuits in federal court rather than state court?
qa_pairs.answer: Plaintiffs' attorneys may prefer to file lawsuits in federal court for several reasons. Firstly, federal court procedures are often more efficient than those in state courts, leading to less crowded dockets and faster case progression to trial. Additionally, federal courts may offer higher average judgments for plaintiffs compared to local state courts. Another factor is the home-court advantage that in-state plaintiffs might have in state courts, which can be mitigated by filing in federal court. Furthermore, the higher status associated with practicing before the federal bench and the possibility of more favorable outcomes for plaintiffs are also motivating factors for plaintiffs' attorneys to pursue diversity cases in federal courts.

One familiar limited jurisdiction court is the small claims court, with jurisdiction to hear civil cases 
involving claims for amounts ranging between $1,000 and $5,000 in about half the states and for 
considerably less in the other states ($500 to $1,000). The advantage of the small claims court is that its 
procedures are informal, it is often located in a neighborhood outside the business district, it is usually 
open after business hours, and it is speedy. Lawyers are not necessary to present the case and in some 
states are not allowed to appear in court. 
 
General Jurisdiction Courts 
All other civil and criminal cases are heard in the general trial courts, or courts of general jurisdiction. 
These go by a variety of names: superior, circuit, district, or common pleas court (New York calls its 
general trial court the supreme court). These are the courts in which people seek redress for incidents 
such as automobile accidents and injuries, or breaches of contract. These state courts also prosecute those 
accused of murder, rape, robbery, and other serious crimes. The fact finder in these general jurisdiction 
courts is not a judge, as in the lower courts, but a jury of citizens. 
 
Although courts of general jurisdiction can hear all types of cases, in most states more than half involve 
family matters (divorce, child custody disputes, and the like). A third were commercial cases, and slightly 
over 10 percent were devoted to car accident cases and other torts (as discussed in Chapter 7 
"Introduction to Tort Law"). 
 
Most states have specialized courts that hear only a certain type of case, such as landlord-tenant disputes 
or probate of wills. Decisions by judges in specialized courts are usually final, although any party 
dissatisfied with the outcome may be able to get a new trial in a court of general jurisdiction. Because 
there has been one trial already, this is known as a trial de novo. It is not an appeal, since the case 
essentially starts over.

qa_pairs.question: What is the jurisdictional limit for civil cases in small claims court in most states, and what are the advantages of these courts?
qa_pairs.answer: In most states, the jurisdictional limit for civil cases in small claims court ranges between $1,000 and $5,000, with some states having a lower limit of $500 to $1,000. The advantages of small claims courts include informal procedures, which make the process less intimidating and more accessible to individuals without legal representation. These courts are often located in neighborhood areas outside the business district, making them more convenient for the public. Additionally, small claims courts are known for their speed, as they aim to resolve disputes quickly. In some states, lawyers are not allowed to appear in court, which further simplifies the process for those who are representing themselves.

qa_pairs.question: What types of cases are typically heard in courts of general jurisdiction, and what is the role of a jury in these courts?
qa_pairs.answer: Courts of general jurisdiction, also known as superior, circuit, district, or common pleas courts, handle a wide range of civil and criminal cases. These include family matters such as divorce and child custody disputes, commercial cases, and serious crimes like murder, rape, and robbery. In these courts, the fact finder is a jury of citizens, which distinguishes them from lower courts where judges serve as fact finders. The jury's role is to listen to the evidence presented by both parties, deliberate, and then reach a verdict based on the facts of the case. This jury system ensures that the decision-making process is a collective effort, reflecting the community's standards and values.

Appellate Courts 
The losing party in a general jurisdiction court can almost always appeal to either one or two higher 
courts. These intermediate appellate courts—usually called courts of appeal—have been established in

procedurally correct manner and whether the appropriate law was applied. For example, the appellant 
(the losing party who appeals) might complain that the judge wrongly instructed the jury on the meaning 
of the law, or improperly allowed testimony of a particular witness, or misconstrued the law in question. 
The appellee (who won in the lower court) will ask that the appellant be denied—usually this means that 
the appellee wants the lower-court judgment affirmed. The appellate court has quite a few choices: it can 
affirm, modify, reverse, or reverse and remand the lower court (return the case to the lower court for 
retrial). 
 
The last type of appeal within the state courts system is to the highest court, the state supreme court, 
which is composed of a single panel of between five and nine judges and is usually located in the state 
capital. (The intermediate appellate courts are usually composed of panels of three judges and are situated 
in various locations around the state.) In a few states, the highest court goes by a different name: in New 
York, it is known as the court of appeals. In certain cases, appellants to the highest court in a state have 
the right to have their appeals heard, but more often the supreme court selects the cases it wishes to hear. 
For most litigants, the ruling of the state supreme court is final. In a relatively small class of cases—those 
in which federal constitutional claims are made—appeal to the US Supreme Court to issue 
a writ of certiorari remains a possibility.

qa_pairs.question: What is a trial de novo and how does it differ from an appeal in the general jurisdiction court system?
qa_pairs.answer: A trial de novo is a new trial that takes place in a court of general jurisdiction, typically after a party is dissatisfied with the outcome of a previous trial. Unlike an appeal, where the appellate court reviews the trial court's decision for procedural correctness and proper application of the law, a trial de novo essentially starts the case over from scratch. The appellate court does not retry the evidence or re-evaluate the facts of the case; instead, it focuses on whether the trial was conducted according to legal procedures and whether the correct laws were applied. The trial de novo allows for a fresh examination of the case, providing an opportunity for a different outcome.

qa_pairs.question: How does the appellate court in the state court system determine the outcome of an appeal, and what are the possible decisions it can make?
qa_pairs.answer: In the state court system, the appellate court reviews the case to determine if the trial was conducted in a procedurally correct manner and if the appropriate law was applied. The appellant, who is the losing party in the lower court, may argue that the judge made errors, such as wrongly instructing the jury, improperly allowing testimony, or misconstruing the law. The appellee, who won in the lower court, seeks to have the lower-court judgment affirmed. The appellate court has several options: it can affirm the lower court's decision, modify it, reverse it, or reverse and remand the case back to the lower court for retrial. The court's decision is based on the legal arguments presented and the evidence from the original trial, but it does not involve re-examining the factual evidence.

qa_pairs.question: How many federal district courts are there in the United States, and how are they distributed among the states?
qa_pairs.answer: There are forty-four federal district courts in the United States, distributed among the states based on their population. Less populous states have one federal district court, while more populous states, such as California, Texas, and New York, have four federal district courts each. This distribution ensures that the federal judicial system can adequately handle the caseload in each state, with the US District Court for the Southern District of New York (Manhattan) being the one with the heaviest commercial docket.

qa_pairs.question: What is the role of the US Supreme Court in the federal judicial system, and how does it exercise control over the courts?
qa_pairs.answer: The US Supreme Court, located in Washington, DC, oversees all federal courts and consists of nine justices, including the chief justice and eight associate justices. Its role is to ensure the uniform interpretation and application of federal law across the United States. The Supreme Court exercises selective control over its docket, meaning it chooses only a small fraction of the cases that are presented to it. This selective process allows the Court to focus on cases of significant legal importance, constitutional issues, or those that have caused conflicting decisions in lower courts. By doing so, the Supreme Court ensures that federal law is consistently applied and that the rights and liberties of individuals are protected. The Court's decisions set precedents that lower courts must follow, thereby maintaining the integrity and coherence of the federal judicial system.

qa_pairs.answer: The number nine is significant in the context of the Supreme Court because it represents the total number of justices, including the Chief Justice and eight associate justices. This number is not constitutionally required; Congress has the authority to establish any number of justices. However, the number has been set at nine since after the Civil War. qa_pairs.question: How does the Supreme Court's control over its docket affect the number of cases it hears, and what was the situation in 2008?
qa_pairs.answer: The Supreme Court has selective control over its docket, meaning it chooses which cases to hear from the many petitions submitted to it. Jurisdiction is an essential concept in understanding courts and the legal system. Jurisdiction is a 
combination of two Latin words: juris (law) and diction(to speak). Which court has the power “to 
speak the law” is the basic question of jurisdiction. 
 
There are two questions about jurisdiction in each case that must be answered before a judge will 
hear a case: the question of subject matter jurisdiction and the question of personal jurisdiction. 
We will consider the question of subject matter jurisdiction first, because judges do; if they

State courts have their origins in colonial era courts. After the American Revolution, state courts 
functioned (with some differences) much like they did in colonial times. The big difference after 1789 was 
that state courts coexisted with federal courts. Federalism was the system devised by the nation’s 
founders in which power is shared between states and the federal government. This sharing requires a 
division of labor between the states and the federal government. It is Article III of the US Constitution 
that spells out the respective spheres of authority (jurisdiction) between state and federal courts. 
 
Take a close look at Article III of the Constitution. (You can find a printable copy of the Constitution 
at http://www.findlaw.com.) Article III makes clear that federal courts are courts of limited power or 
jurisdiction. Notice that the only kinds of cases federal courts are authorized to deal with have strong 
federal connections. For example, federal courts have jurisdiction when a federal law is being used by the 
plaintiff or prosecutor (a “federal question” case) or the case arises “in admiralty” (meaning that the

qa_pairs.question: What is the concept of subject matter jurisdiction and how does it differ from personal jurisdiction?
qa_pairs.answer: Subject matter jurisdiction refers to the authority of a court to hear and decide cases of a particular type or cases relating to a specific subject matter. It is a fundamental aspect of jurisdiction that determines whether a court has the power to hear a case based on the nature of the legal issues involved. Personal jurisdiction, on the other hand, pertains to the court's power over the parties involved in the case. It requires that the court have authority over the individuals or entities being sued or sued against, which is typically established through their presence or activities within the court's geographic area. While subject matter jurisdiction focuses on the type of case a court can hear, personal jurisdiction deals with the court's power over the parties involved. A court must have both subject matter jurisdiction and personal jurisdiction to properly hear and decide a case.

qa_pairs.question: How does the US Constitution provide instructions on the jurisdiction of federal courts, and what types of cases must be heard in federal courts only?
qa_pairs.answer: The US Constitution, specifically Article III, outlines the jurisdiction of federal courts. It establishes that federal courts have limited jurisdiction, meaning they can only hear cases that have a strong federal connection. Federal courts have jurisdiction over cases involving federal laws (federal question jurisdiction) and cases arising in admiralty (maritime law). Additionally, federal courts have exclusive jurisdiction over certain types of cases, such as those involving the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties, as well as cases involving disputes between states or between a state and the federal government. These exclusive jurisdiction cases must be heard in federal courts only. The Constitution also provides for diversity of citizenship jurisdiction, which allows federal courts to hear cases where the parties are from different states or countries, and the amount in controversy exceeds a certain threshold. This ensures that federal courts can provide a neutral forum for resolving disputes between parties from different jurisdictions.

qa_pairs.question: Why are state courts typically the ones to handle disputes such as auto accidents between residents of different states?

times through Independence and to the present. (See also Chapter 7 "Introduction to Tort Law" of this 
text.) People have had a need to resolve this kind of dispute long before our federal courts were created, 
and you can tell from Article III that the founders did not specify that tort or negligence claims should be 
handled by the federal courts. Again, federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction, limited to the kinds 
of cases specified in Article III. If the case before the federal court does not fall within one of those 
categories, the federal court cannot constitutionally hear the case because it does not have subject matter 
jurisdiction. 
 
Always remember: a court must have subject matter jurisdiction to hear and decide a case. Without it, a 
court cannot address the merits of the controversy or even take the next jurisdictional step of figuring out 
which of the defendants can be sued in that court. The question of which defendants are appropriately 
before the court is a question of personal jurisdiction. 
 
Because there are two court systems, it is important for a plaintiff to file in the right court to begin with. 
The right court is the one that has subject matter jurisdiction over the case—that is, the power to hear and 
decide the kind of case that is filed. Not only is it a waste of time to file in the wrong court system and be 
dismissed, but if the dismissal comes after the filing period imposed by the

qa_pairs.question: Why would state courts typically resolve disputes where parties blame each other for an accident?
qa_pairs.answer: State courts would typically resolve disputes where parties blame each other for an accident because such disputes often involve tort claims, specifically negligence. Negligence is a primary element of tort law, which has been a part of the legal system since British colonial times through Independence and to the present. Federal courts, on the other hand, have limited jurisdiction and are only empowered to hear cases that fall within specific categories outlined in Article III of the Constitution. Since tort or negligence claims do not fall within these categories, federal courts cannot constitutionally hear such cases. Therefore, when individuals allege that the other party's fault caused an accident, they are essentially starting a tort case, which state courts are well-equipped to handle. State courts have a long history of dealing with tort claims, making them the appropriate venue for resolving such disputes.

qa_pairs.question: What is the significance of subject matter jurisdiction in the context of filing a lawsuit in the correct court system?
qa_pairs.answer: Subject matter jurisdiction is crucial when filing a lawsuit because it determines whether a court has the authority to hear and decide a particular type of case. Without subject matter jurisdiction, a court cannot address the merits of the controversy or even proceed to determine which defendants can be sued in that court. This is a fundamental aspect of personal jurisdiction, which is the court's power to make decisions affecting the parties involved. If a plaintiff files a lawsuit in the wrong court system, it is not only a waste of time but also risks the case being dismissed. More importantly, if the dismissal occurs after the statute of limitations has expired, the plaintiff may lose the opportunity to refile the case in the correct court system. This could result in the case being permanently dismissed, regardless of the plaintiff's merits. Therefore, understanding and ensuring that the correct court system with the appropriate subject matter jurisdiction is chosen at the outset is essential for the successful pursuit of justice.

qa_pairs.answer: A case with a federal question can be heard in either state or federal court based on the principle of concurrent jurisdiction. qa_pairs.question: Under what conditions can a federal court have subject matter jurisdiction over a case based on state law?

qa_pairs.question: What are the requirements for a federal court to have subject matter jurisdiction over a case based on state law?
qa_pairs.answer: A federal court will have subject matter jurisdiction over any case based on state law if two conditions are met: (1) the parties involved must be from different states, ensuring complete diversity of citizenship between all plaintiffs and defendants, and (2) the amount in controversy must be at least $75,000. qa_pairs.question: How does the choice of law process work in diversity cases, and why might it be significant?
qa_pairs.answer: In diversity cases, the choice of law process determines which state's law will be applied to resolve the legal rights and responsibilities of the parties involved. This process is governed by each state's own set of judicial decisions that address conflict of laws. For instance, if a lawsuit is filed in Texas but the incident occurred in New Mexico, the Texas court may still apply New Mexico law because it governs the specific circumstances of the case, such as motor vehicle laws and accidents. The significance of the choice of law process lies in the fact that different states may have varying substantive law standards, which can greatly influence the outcome of a case. For example, in a breach of contract case, the version of the Uniform Commercial Code applied can differ from state to state, potentially benefiting one party over another. In the scenario of Anna v. To better understand subject matter jurisdiction in action, let’s take an example. Wile E. Coyote wants a 
federal judge to hear his products-liability action against Acme, Inc., even though the action is based on 
state law. Mr. Coyote’s attorney wants to “make a federal case” out of it, thinking that the jurors in the 
federal district court’s jury pool will understand the case better and be more likely to deliver a “high value”

and has its principal place of business in Chicago, Illinois. The federal court in Arizona can hear and 
decide Mr. Coyote’s case (i.e., it has subject matter jurisdiction over the case) because of diversity of 
citizenship. If Mr. Coyote was injured by one of Acme’s defective products while chasing a roadrunner in 
Arizona, the federal district court judge would hear his action—using federal procedural law—and decide 
the case based on the substantive law of Arizona on product liability.

business in Phoenix, Arizona. Unless Mr. Coyote has a federal law he is using as a basis for his claims 
against Acme, his attempt to get a federal court to hear and decide the case will fail. It will fail because 
there is not complete diversity of citizenship between the plaintiff and the defendant.
