to attempt to clarify, simplify, and improve the law. One of its first projects, and ultimately one of its most 
successful, was the drafting of the Restatement of the Law of Contracts, completed in 1932. A 
revision—the Restatement (Second) of Contracts—was undertaken in 1946 and finally completed in 1979. 
The Restatements (others exist in the fields of torts, agency, conflicts of laws, judgments, property, 
restitution, security, and trusts) are detailed analyses of the decided cases in the field. These analyses are 
made with an eye to discerning the various principles that have emerged from the courts, and to the 
maximum extent possible, the Restatements declare the law as the courts have determined it to be. The 
Restatements, guided by a Reporter (the director of the project) and a staff of legal scholars, go through 
several so-called “tentative” drafts—sometimes as many as fifteen or twenty—and are screened by various 
committees within the American Law Institute before they are eventually published as final documents. 
 
The Restatement of Contracts won prompt respect in the courts and has been cited in innumerable cases. 
The Restatements are not authoritative, in the sense that they are not actual judicial precedents, but they 
are nevertheless weighty interpretive texts, and judges frequently look to them for guidance. They are as 
close to “black letter” rules of law as exist anywhere in the American legal system for judge-made 
(common) law.

qa_pairs.question: What is the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) and how does it relate to the American Law Institute?
qa_pairs.answer: The Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) is a model law developed by the American Law Institute and the National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws. It has been adopted in one form or another in all fifty states, the District of Columbia, and the American territories. The UCC is significant because it provides a consistent set of rules governing commercial transactions, particularly the sale of goods, across different states. Before the UCC was written, commercial law varied greatly from state to state, which posed a nuisance and later became a serious impediment to business as the American economy grew. The UCC, therefore, represents a major effort by the American Law Institute to standardize and simplify commercial law across the United States.

Before the UCC was written, commercial law varied, sometimes greatly, from state to state. This first 
proved a nuisance and then a serious impediment to business as the American economy became 
nationwide during the twentieth century. Although there had been some uniform laws concerned with 
commercial deals—including the Uniform Sales Act, first published in 1906—few were widely adopted and 
none nationally. As a result, the law governing sales of goods, negotiable instruments, warehouse receipts, 
securities, and other matters crucial to doing business in an industrial, market economy was a crazy quilt 
of untidy provisions that did not mesh well from state to state. 
 
Initial drafting of the UCC began in 1942 and was ten years in the making, involving the efforts of 
hundreds of practicing lawyers, law teachers, and judges. A final draft, promulgated by the Institute and 
the Conference, was endorsed by the American Bar Association and published in 1951. 
 
Pennsylvania enacted the code in its entirety in 1953. It was the only state to enact the original version, 
because the Law Revision Commission of the New York State legislature began to examine it line by line 
and had serious objections. Three years later, in 1956, a revised code was issued. This version, known as 
the 1957 Official Text, was enacted in Massachusetts and Kentucky. In 1958, the Conference and the 
Institute amended the Code further and again reissued it, this time as the 1958 Official Text. Sixteen 
states, including Pennsylvania, adopted this version. 
 
But in so doing, many of these states changed particular provisions. As a consequence, the Uniform 
Commercial Code was no longer so uniform. Responding to this development the American Law Institute 
established a permanent editorial board to oversee future revisions of the code. Various subcommittees 
went to work redrafting, and a 1962 Official Text was eventually published. Twelve more states adopted

qa_pairs.question: What are the different articles of the UCC and what do they cover?
qa_pairs.answer: The UCC is organized into several 'articles', each covering a different aspect of commercial transactions. Article 2 deals with Sales, Article 3 with Commercial Paper, Article 4 with Bank Deposits and Collections, Article 5 with Letters of Credit, Article 6 with Bulk Transfers, Article 7 with Warehouse Receipts, Bills of Lading, and Other Documents of Title, Article 8 with Investment Securities, and Article 9 with Secured Transactions; Sales of Accounts and Chattel Paper. We now turn our attention to the sale—the first facet, and the cornerstone, of the commercial transaction. 
Sales law is a special type of contract law in that Article 2 applies only to the sale of goods, defined 
(Section 2-105) in part as “all things . . . which are movable at the time of identification to the contract for 
sale other than the money in which the price is to be paid. . . .” The only contracts and agreements covered 
by Article 2 are those relating to the present or future sale of goods. 
 
In certain cases, the courts have difficulty in determining the nature of the object of a sales contract. The 
problem: How can goods and services be separated in contracts calling for the seller to deliver a 
combination of goods and services? This difficulty frequently arises in product liability cases in which the 
buyer sues the seller for breach of one of the UCC warranties. For example, you go to the hairdresser for a 
permanent and the shampoo gives you a severe scalp rash. May you recover damages on the grounds that 
either the hairdresser or the manufacturer breached an implied warranty in the sale of goods? 
 
When the goods used are incidental to the service, the courts are split on whether the plaintiff should win. 
Compare Epstein v. Giannattasio, 197 A.2d 342 (Conn. 1963), in which the court held that no sale of 
goods had been made because the plaintiff received a treatment in which the cosmetics were only 
incidentally used, with Newmark v. Gimbel’s Inc., 258 A.2d 697 (N.J. 1969), in which the court said “[i]f 
the permanent wave lotion were sold … for home consumption . . . unquestionably an implied warranty of 
fitness for that purpose would have been an integral incident of the sale.” The New Jersey court rejected 
the defendant’s argument that by actually applying the lotion to the patron’s head the salon lessened the 
liability it otherwise would have had if it had simply sold her the lotion.

resolved the issue through legislation. One area involves restaurant cases, in which typically the plaintiff

qa_pairs.answer: Under Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), 'goods' are defined as 'all things . . . which are movable at the time of identification to the contract for sale other than the money in which the price is to be paid.' This definition encompasses a wide range of items, including tangible personal property that can be moved. Article 2 specifically applies to contracts for the present or future sale of goods, making it a specialized area of contract law focused on transactions involving movable items. qa_pairs.question: How do courts determine whether a contract involves the sale of goods or a combination of goods and services, and what are some examples of cases that illustrate this issue?
qa_pairs.answer: Courts face challenges in determining whether a contract involves the sale of goods or a combination of goods and services, especially when the contract includes both elements. The primary issue is distinguishing between the goods and the services provided in the contract. For instance, in product liability cases, a buyer may sue a seller for breach of warranty after experiencing harm from a product used in conjunction with a service, such as a permanent hair treatment. Gimbel’s Inc., the court found that the sale of goods was integral to the contract because the permanent wave lotion was sold for home consumption. State legislatures have also intervened in some cases, such as restaurant cases, by explicitly declaring that serving food or drink constitutes a sale of goods, thereby invoking the implied warranty of merchantability under UCC Section 2-314(1).

Three Basic Contract Types: Sources of Law 
With this brief description of the UCC, it should now be clear that the primary sources of law for the three 
basic types of contracts are: 
 
• 
Real estate: common law; 
• 
Services: common law; 
• 
Sale of goods: UCC (as interpreted by the courts). 
 
Common law and UCC rules are often similar. For example, both require good faith in the performance of 
a contract. However, there are two general differences worth noting between the common law of contracts 
and the UCC’s rules governing the sales of goods. First, the UCC is more liberal than the common law in 
upholding the existence of a contract. For example, in a sales contract (covered by the UCC), “open” 
terms—that is, those the parties have not agreed upon—do not require a court to rule that no contract was 
made. However, open terms in a nonsales contract will frequently result in a ruling that there is no 
contract. Second, although the common law of contracts applies to every person equally, under the UCC 
“merchants” occasionally receive special treatment. By “merchants” the UCC means persons who have 
special knowledge or skill who deal in the goods involved in the transaction.

The Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods 
A Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (CISG) was approved in 1980 at 
a diplomatic conference in Vienna. (A convention is a preliminary agreement that serves as the basis for a 
formal treaty.) The Convention has been adopted by several countries, including the United States. 
 
The Convention is significant for three reasons. First, the Convention is a uniform law governing the sale 
of goods—in effect, an international Uniform Commercial Code. The major goal of the drafters was to 
produce a uniform law acceptable to countries with different legal, social and economic systems. Second, 
although provisions in the Convention are generally consistent with the UCC, there are significant 
differences. For instance, under the Convention, consideration (discussed below) is not required to form a 
contract and there is no Statute of Frauds (a requirement that some contracts be evidenced by a writing to 
be enforceable—also discussed below). Finally, the Convention represents the first attempt by the US 
Senate to reform the private law of business through its treaty powers, for the Convention preempts the 
UCC if the parties to a contract elect to use the CISG. 
 
Basic Contract Taxonomy 
Contracts are not all cut from the same die. Some are written, some oral; some are explicit, some not. 
Because contracts can be formed, expressed, and enforced in a variety of ways, a taxonomy of contracts 
has developed that is useful in lumping together like legal consequences. In general, contracts are 
classified along these dimensions: explicitness, mutuality, enforceability, and degree of 
completion. Explicitness is concerned with the degree to which the agreement is manifest to those not 
party to it. Mutuality takes into account whether promises are exchanged by two parties or only 
one. Enforceability is the degree to which a given contract is binding. Completion considers whether 
the contract is yet to be performed or the obligations have been fully discharged by one or both parties. 
We will examine each of these concepts in turn.

qa_pairs.answer: The Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (CISG), approved in 1980 at a diplomatic conference in Vienna, is significant for several reasons. Firstly, it serves as a uniform law governing the sale of goods, effectively acting as an international Uniform Commercial Code. The primary goal of the drafters was to create a uniform law that would be acceptable to countries with diverse legal, social, and economic systems. Secondly, while the CISG's provisions are generally consistent with the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), there are notable differences. For example, under the CISG, consideration is not required to form a contract, and there is no Statute of Frauds, which is a requirement in the UCC that some contracts must be evidenced by a writing to be enforceable. Lastly, the CISG represents the first attempt by the US Senate to reform the private law of business through its treaty powers. It preempts the UCC if the parties to a contract elect to use the CISG, making it a significant tool for international trade.

qa_pairs.question: How are contracts classified according to the basic contract taxonomy discussed in the text?
qa_pairs.answer: Contracts are classified according to the basic contract taxonomy along four dimensions: explicitness, mutuality, enforceability, and degree of completion. Explicitness refers to the degree to which the agreement is clear and manifest to those not party to it, distinguishing between express contracts, where terms are directly stated, and implied contracts, where terms are inferred from actions or circumstances. Mutuality considers whether promises are exchanged by two parties or only one, leading to bilateral contracts, which involve mutual promises, and unilateral contracts, which involve a promise in exchange for an act. Enforceability assesses the degree to which a contract is binding and legally enforceable. Finally, the degree of completion looks at whether the contract is yet to be performed or if the obligations have been fully discharged by one or both parties, distinguishing between executory contracts, which are yet to be performed, and executed contracts, where obligations have been fulfilled. This taxonomy helps in understanding the legal consequences and obligations associated with different types of contracts.

An express contract is one in which the terms are spelled out directly; the parties to an express 
contract, whether written or oral, are conscious that they are making an enforceable agreement. For 
example, an agreement to purchase your neighbor’s car for $500 and to take title next Monday is an

Implied Contract 
An implied contract is one that is inferred from the actions of the parties. Although no discussion of 
terms took place, an implied contract exists if it is clear from the conduct of both parties that they 
intended there be one. A delicatessen patron who asks for a “turkey sandwich to go” has made a contract 
and is obligated to pay when the sandwich is made. By ordering the food, the patron is implicitly agreeing 
to the price, whether posted or not. 
 
Contract Implied in Law: Quasi-contract 
Both express and implied contracts embody an actual agreement of the parties. A quasi-contract, by 
contrast, is an obligation said to be ‘‘imposed by law” in order to avoid unjust enrichment of one person at 
the expense of another. In fact, a quasi-contract is not a contract at all; it is a fiction that the courts 
created to prevent injustice. Suppose, for example, that a carpenter mistakenly believes you have hired 
him to repair your porch; in fact, it is your neighbor who has hired him. One Saturday morning he arrives 
at your doorstep and begins to work. Rather than stop him, you let him proceed, pleased at the prospect of 
having your porch fixed for free (since you have never talked to the carpenter, you figure you need not pay 
his bill). Although it is true there is no contract, the law implies a contract for the value of the work.

qa_pairs.question: What is an express contract and can you provide an example of it?
qa_pairs.answer: An express contract is a type of contract where the terms are explicitly stated, either in writing or orally, making the parties aware that they are entering into an enforceable agreement. For instance, if you agree to purchase your neighbor's car for $500 and take title next Monday, this agreement constitutes an express contract. The terms of the contract, including the price and the time for taking title, are clearly communicated and agreed upon by both parties.

qa_pairs.question: What is a quasi-contract and how does it differ from express and implied contracts?
qa_pairs.answer: A quasi-contract, also known as an implied-in-law contract, is not a true contract but a legal construct created by courts to prevent unjust enrichment of one party at the expense of another. Unlike express and implied contracts, which involve actual agreements between parties, a quasi-contract is imposed by law. For example, if a carpenter mistakenly repairs your porch thinking you hired him, and you let him proceed without correcting his mistake, the law implies a contract for the value of the work done. This is to ensure that the carpenter is compensated for his services, even though there was no actual agreement between you and him. The key difference is that a quasi-contract is not based on the mutual promises of the parties but is a legal fiction to prevent injustice.

Enforceability 
Not every agreement between two people is a binding contract. An agreement that is lacking one of the 
legal elements of a contract is said to be void—that is, not a contract at all. An agreement that is illegal—
for example, a promise to commit a crime in return for a money payment—is void. Neither party to a void 
“contract” may enforce it. 
 
By contrast, a voidable contract is one that is unenforceable by one party but enforceable by the other. 
For example, a minor (any person under eighteen, in most states) may “avoid” a contract with an adult; 
the adult may not enforce the contract against the minor, if the minor refuses to carry out the bargain. But 
the adult has no choice if the minor wishes the contract to be performed. (A contract may be voidable by 
both parties if both are minors.) Ordinarily, the parties to a voidable contract are entitled to be restored to 
their original condition. Suppose you agree to buy your seventeen-year-old neighbor’s car. He delivers it 
to you in exchange for your agreement to pay him next week. He has the legal right to terminate the deal 
and recover the car, in which case you will of course have no obligation to pay him. If you have already 
paid him, he still may legally demand a return to the status quo ante (previous state of affairs). You must 
return the car to him; he must return the cash to you. 
A voidable contract remains a valid contract until it is voided. Thus, a contract with a minor remains in 
force unless the minor decides he does not wish to be bound by it. When the minor reaches his majority, 
he may “ratify” the contract—that is, agree to be bound by it-in which case the contract will no longer be 
voidable and will thereafter be fully enforceable.

qa_pairs.question: What is a unilateral contract and can you provide an example of it?
qa_pairs.answer: A unilateral contract is a type of agreement where only one party makes a promise, and the contract becomes binding only upon the performance of that promise. For instance, if Charles offers Fran $5 to wash his car, Charles is contractually bound to pay Fran once she washes the car. Fran does not make a promise to Charles, but by performing the act of washing the car, she makes Charles liable to pay him the agreed amount. Another common example of a unilateral contract is an offer of $50 for the return of a lost dog. In this case, Frances does not promise to return the dog, but if she finds and returns the dog, she is entitled to the $50.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a void contract and a voidable contract, and can you provide an example of each?
qa_pairs.answer: A void contract is an agreement that lacks one of the legal elements of a contract and is therefore not enforceable by either party. For example, a contract promising to commit a crime in return for money is void because it is illegal. Neither party can enforce such a contract. On the other hand, a voidable contract is one that is unenforceable by one party but enforceable by the other. For instance, a contract with a minor is voidable because the minor has the legal right to terminate the deal and recover any goods or money exchanged. If the minor decides to continue with the contract, it becomes fully enforceable. Another example of a voidable contract is a contract with a mentally incapacitated person, where the contract can be voided by the incapacitated person or their legal guardian.

outset. Whether a valid enforceable contract has been formed depends in turn on whether:

qa_pairs.question: What did Sir Henry Maine mean when he wrote of society’s movement 'from status to contract'?
qa_pairs.answer: Sir Henry Maine, in his seminal work 'Ancient Law' (1869), discussed the evolution of society from a structure where individuals' roles and rights were determined by their status within a rigid hierarchy, to one where relationships and obligations are governed by contracts. This transition signifies a shift from a society where one's position and duties are ascribed by birth or tradition, to one where individuals have the freedom to enter into agreements and contracts based on mutual consent. Maine's observation highlights the increasing importance of personal autonomy and the legal recognition of agreements made between parties as the foundation of social and economic interactions.

qa_pairs.question: Are all promises 'contracts'?
qa_pairs.answer: Not all promises constitute contracts. For a promise to be considered a contract, it must meet certain legal criteria. These criteria include mutuality of agreement, where both parties must have a clear understanding and agreement on the terms; consideration, which means that something of value must be exchanged between the parties; legality, ensuring that the contract's purpose is lawful; capacity, meaning that the parties must have the legal ability to enter into a contract; and proper form, which may require the contract to be in writing depending on the jurisdiction and the nature of the agreement. A mere promise without these elements does not create a legally binding contract.

Consideration, is the quid pro quo (something given or received for something else) between the 
contracting parties in the absence of which the law will not enforce the promise or promises made. 
Consider the following three “contracts”: 
 
1. Betty offers to give a book to Lou. Lou accepts. 
2. Betty offers Lou the book in exchange for Lou’s promise to pay $15. Lou accepts. 
3. Betty offers to give Lou the book if Lou promises to pick it up at Betty’s house. Lou accepts. 
 
The question is which, if any, is a binding contract? In American law, only situation 2 is a binding 
contract, because only that contract contains a set of mutual promises in which each party pledges to give 
up something to the benefit of the other. 
 
The question of what constitutes a binding contract has been answered differently throughout history and 
in other cultures. For example, under Roman law, any contract that was reduced to writing was binding, 
whether or not there was consideration in our sense. Moreover, in later Roman times, certain promises of 
gifts were made binding, whether written or oral; these would not be binding in the United States. And in 
the Anglo-American tradition, the presence of a seal was once sufficient to make a contract binding 
without any other consideration. In most states, the seal is no longer a substitute for consideration, 
although in some states it creates a presumption of consideration. The Uniform Commercial Code has 
abolished the seal on contracts for the sale of goods.

qa_pairs.question: What is the 'mailbox rule' and how does it affect the effectiveness of an acceptance in contract law?
qa_pairs.answer: The 'mailbox rule' is a legal principle in contract law that determines when an acceptance of an offer becomes effective. According to this rule, an acceptance is considered effective upon dispatch, meaning when it is sent, rather than when it is received by the offeror. This principle has its roots in English courts and dates back nearly two hundred years. The mailbox rule is particularly significant in situations where the method of transmission used to send the acceptance is not instantaneous, such as postal mail. Under this rule, if an acceptance is sent in a manner that is considered reasonable and in accordance with the method of communication stipulated by the offeror, the acceptance is deemed effective at the moment it is placed in the mail, even if the offeror has not yet received it. This rule ensures that the offeree's acceptance is legally binding once it has been properly dispatched, providing clarity and certainty in contractual agreements.

qa_pairs.question: How does the concept of consideration affect the formation of a binding contract in American law?
qa_pairs.answer: In American law, consideration is a fundamental element required for the formation of a binding contract. Consideration refers to the quid pro quo, or the exchange of something of value, between the contracting parties. It is the mutual exchange that each party pledges to give up for the benefit of the other. For a contract to be enforceable, there must be a set of mutual promises, where each party provides something of value, whether it be an act, forbearance, or a promise. Without consideration, a promise or agreement is not legally binding. For example, in the given scenarios, only the second contract, where Betty offers Lou the book in exchange for Lou's promise to pay $15, constitutes a binding contract because it involves a clear exchange of promises. The first contract, where Betty simply offers to give Lou a book without any reciprocal obligation, lacks consideration and is not enforceable. Similarly, the third contract, where Betty's offer is contingent upon Lou's promise to pick up the book, also lacks the mutual exchange of promises and is not considered a binding contract. The concept of consideration ensures that both parties have a vested interest in the contract and that there is a tangible exchange of value, which is essential for the contract's enforceability.

qa_pairs.question: What are the two elements that constitute legally sufficient consideration in a contract?
qa_pairs.answer: Legally sufficient consideration in a contract consists of two elements: (1) the promisee must incur a legal detriment, which means they must give up a legal right or benefit, and (2) the legal detriment must be bargained for, meaning the promisor must have specifically intended the act, forbearance, or promise in return for their promise. The first element focuses on whether the promisee has given up something of legal value, which could be an act, forbearance, or a promise of such. The second element examines the intent behind the promise, ensuring that the promisee's legal detriment was indeed sought by the promisor as a condition for their promise. This two-pronged test helps determine whether the consideration is legally sufficient, as it ensures that there is a mutual exchange of value between the parties involved in the contract.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances will the courts enforce a promise without consideration according to the doctrine of promissory estoppel?
qa_pairs.answer: The courts will enforce a promise without consideration under the doctrine of promissory estoppel when three specific conditions are met: (1) the promise is one that the promisor should reasonably expect to induce the promisee to take action or forbear from taking action, (2) the promisee actually does take such action or forbearance, and (3) injustice can only be avoided by enforcing the promise. Promissory estoppel is invoked in the interests of justice to prevent the promisor from arguing that there was no consideration when the promisee has relied on the promise to their detriment. This doctrine ensures fairness and prevents the promisor from escaping their obligations when their promise has led to a significant change in the promisee's position. It is a legal principle that allows the courts to enforce promises to prevent injustice, even in the absence of traditional consideration.

qa_pairs.answer: Promissory estoppel is a legal doctrine that prevents a promisor from denying the existence of a promise when the promisee has reasonably relied on that promise to their detriment. According to the text segment, promissory estoppel can be invoked when three specific conditions are met: (1) the promise made by the promisor should reasonably be expected to induce the promisee to take action or refrain from taking action of a definite and substantial character; (2) the promisee actually takes such action or refrains from taking action; and (3) injustice can only be avoided by enforcing the promise. qa_pairs.question: What is the primary purpose of the Statute of Frauds, as enacted in England in 1677?

qa_pairs.question: What are the three principal remedies available for a breach of contract?
qa_pairs.answer: The three principal remedies available for a breach of contract are monetary awards (also known as damages), specific performance, and restitution. Monetary awards are designed to compensate the injured party for the loss incurred due to the breach. This can include compensatory damages, which aim to put the injured party in the position they would have been in had the contract been performed, and punitive damages, which are intended to punish the breaching party for particularly egregious behavior. Specific performance is a remedy where the court orders the breaching party to fulfill their contractual obligations as agreed. This remedy is typically reserved for situations where monetary compensation is inadequate, such as in the case of unique goods or real estate. Restitution is another remedy that aims to restore the injured party to the position they were in before the contract was formed. This can involve returning any benefits conferred to the breaching party, ensuring that they do not unjustly enrich themselves at the expense of the injured party.

qa_pairs.question: Why is specific performance considered a remedy in certain cases, and what makes it unique compared to other remedies?
qa_pairs.answer: Specific performance is considered a remedy in certain cases because it is a judicial order that compels the breaching party to fulfill their contractual obligations as originally agreed upon. This remedy is unique compared to other remedies because it goes beyond merely awarding monetary compensation. Specific performance is typically reserved for situations where the subject matter of the contract is unique or irreplaceable, such as in the sale of real estate, rare art, or custom-made goods. In these cases, monetary damages may not adequately compensate the injured party because the value of the unique item cannot be easily quantified or replaced. By ordering the breaching party to perform their contractual duties, the court ensures that the injured party receives the specific performance they were promised, thereby achieving a more just and equitable outcome. This remedy is particularly important in contracts involving unique goods or properties, where the injured party's interests are best served by receiving exactly what was agreed upon rather than a monetary substitute.

numerous occasions on which it would be theoretically possible for courts to order the parties to carry out 
their contracts, the courts will not do it. In 1897, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr., declared in a famous 
line that “the duty to keep a contract at common law means a prediction that you must pay damages if you 
do not keep it.” By that he meant simply that the common law looks more toward compensating the 
promisee for his loss than toward compelling the promisor to perform—a person always has the power, 
though not the right, to breach a contract. Indeed, the law of remedies often provides the parties with an 
incentive to break the contract. In short, the promisor has a choice: to perform or pay. The purpose of 
contract remedies is, for the most part, to compensate the non-breaching party for the losses suffered—to 
put the non-breaching party in the position he, she, or it would have been in had there been no breach. 
 
Compensatory Damages 
One party has the right to damages (money ) when the other party has breached the contract unless, of 
course, the contract itself or other circumstances suspend or discharge that 
right. Compensatory damages is the general category of damages awarded to make the non-breaching 
party whole.

qa_pairs.answer: The primary purpose of compensatory damages in contract law is to make the non-breaching party whole. The goal is to put the non-breaching party in the position they would have been in had the breach not occurred. Compensatory damages are the general category of damages awarded in such cases, and they aim to cover the actual losses incurred by the non-breaching party.

Baxendale, decided in 1854, established the principle that a person injured by a breach of contract is not entitled to compensation unless the breaching party had reason to foresee the loss as a probable result of the breach at the time the contract was made. This principle is known as the foreseeability rule. In the Hadley v. Baxendale case, the court held that the carrier, Pickford and Company, could not be held liable for the delay in delivering the shaft because they had no reason to foresee that the delay would cause the Hadleys to lose profits from their mill. The court emphasized that damages must be reasonably foreseeable and not merely possible or speculative.

and reasonably be considered either arising naturally, i.e., according to the usual course of

for any consequences as long as the breach caused the injury and the plaintiff did not exacerbate

course of things,” a mill would have on hand a spare shaft, so that its operations would not

qa_pairs.question: What are consequential damages and can you provide an example of when a party might be liable for them?
qa_pairs.answer: Consequential damages are damages that flow as a foreseeable consequence of a breach of contract. They are not the direct result of the breach but are secondary effects that the breaching party could reasonably have anticipated. For example, if a roofer is hired to fix a leak in a roof and the poor workmanship leads to water damage inside the house, the roofer would be liable for consequential damages. This could include the cost of repairing ruined drapes, damaged flooring, and walls, among other related damages. The key aspect of consequential damages is that they must be a foreseeable result of the breach at the time the contract was made.

Incidental Damages 
Suppose City College hires Prof. Blake on a two-year contract, after an extensive search. After one year the 
professor quits to take a job elsewhere, in breach of her contract. If City College has to pay $5000 more to 
find a replacement for year, Blake is liable for that amount—that’s compensatory damages. But what if it 
costs City College $1200 to search for, bring to campus and interview a replacement? City College can 
claim that, too, as incidental damages which include additional costs incurred by the non-breaching 
party after the breach in a reasonable attempt to avoid further loss, even if the attempt is unsuccessful. 
 
Punitive Damages 
Punitive damages are those awarded for the purpose of punishing a defendant in a civil action, in 
which criminal sanctions may be unavailable. They are not part of the compensation for the loss suffered; 
they are proper in cases in which the defendant has acted willfully and maliciously and are thought to 
deter others from acting similarly. Since the purpose of contract law is compensation, not punishment, 
punitive damages have not traditionally been awarded, with one exception: when the breach of contract is 
also a tort for which punitive damages may be recovered. Punitive damages are permitted in the law of 
torts (in most states) when the behavior is malicious or willful (reckless conduct causing physical harm, 
deliberate defamation of one’s character, a knowingly unlawful taking of someone’s property), and some 
kinds of contract breach are also tortuous—for example, when a creditor holding collateral as security 
under a contract for a loan sells the collateral to a good-faith purchaser for value even though the debtor 
was not in default, he has breached the contract and committed the tort of conversion. Punitive 
damages may be awarded, assuming the behavior was willful and not merely mistaken. 
 
Punitive damages are not fixed by law. The judge or jury may award at its discretion whatever sum is 
believed necessary to redress the wrong or deter like conduct in the future. This means that a richer 
person may be slapped with much heavier punitive damages than a poorer one in the appropriate case.

qa_pairs.question: What are incidental damages in the context of a breach of contract, and can you provide an example involving City College and Prof. Blake?
qa_pairs.answer: Incidental damages refer to additional costs incurred by the non-breaching party after the breach in a reasonable attempt to avoid further loss, even if the attempt is unsuccessful. For instance, if City College hires Prof. Blake on a two-year contract and she quits after one year, City College may incur additional costs to find a replacement. If it costs City College $1200 to search for, bring to campus, and interview a replacement, this amount can be claimed as incidental damages. These damages are part of the compensatory damages that the breaching party, Prof. Blake, is liable for, as they are directly related to the breach and the efforts made by City College to mitigate the damages.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances can punitive damages be awarded in a breach of contract case, and what is their purpose?
qa_pairs.answer: Punitive damages can be awarded in a breach of contract case when the breach is also a tort for which punitive damages may be recovered, and the defendant's behavior is willful or malicious. The purpose of punitive damages is not to compensate for the loss suffered but to punish the defendant and deter others from acting similarly. They are appropriate in cases where the defendant has acted with reckless conduct causing physical harm, deliberate defamation, or a knowingly unlawful taking of someone’s property. For example, if a creditor holding collateral as security under a contract for a loan sells the collateral to a good-faith purchaser for value even though the debtor was not in default, the creditor has breached the contract and committed the tort of conversion. In such cases, punitive damages may be awarded to punish the creditor for their willful and malicious conduct and to deter similar behavior in the future. The amount of punitive damages is at the discretion of the judge or jury and may be adjusted if deemed excessive.

honor their contracts. Many of these cases involve disability payments, and among the elements are 
charges of tortious conduct by the company’s agents or employees. California has been the leader among 
the state courts in their growing willingness to uphold punitive damage awards despite insurer complaints

Specific Performance 
Specific performance is a judicial order to the promisor that he undertake the performance to which 
he obligated himself in a contract. Specific performance is an alternative remedy to damages and may be 
issued at the discretion of the court, subject to a number of exceptions. (When the promisee is seeking 
enforcement of a contractual provision for forbearance—a promise that the promisor will refrain from 
doing something—an injunction, a judicial order not to act in a specified manner, may be the appropriate 
remedy.) Emily signs a contract to sell Charlotte a gold samovar, a Russian antique of great sentimental 
value because it once belonged to Charlotte’s mother. Emily then repudiates the contract while still 
executory. A court may properly grant Charlotte an order of specific performance against Emily. Specific 
performance is an attractive but limited remedy: it is only available for breach of contract to sell a unique 
item (real estate is always unique). 
 
Restitution 
As the word implies, restitution is a restoring to one party of what he gave to the other. Therefore, only 
to the extent that the injured party conferred a benefit on the other party may the injured party be 
awarded restitution.

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of punitive damages in legal cases, and how can a judge adjust these damages?
qa_pairs.answer: Punitive damages are awarded in legal cases to punish the defendant for particularly egregious or malicious conduct and to deter similar behavior in the future. They are not meant to compensate the plaintiff, but rather to serve as a penalty for the defendant's actions. In some cases, a person may be slapped with much heavier punitive damages than a poorer one, depending on the circumstances of the case. However, the judge has the discretion to remit, or lower, some or all of a punitive damage award if they consider it excessive. This adjustment ensures that the punitive damages are proportionate to the severity of the defendant's conduct and the harm caused.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances might a court grant specific performance as a remedy for breach of contract, and what limitations does this remedy have?
qa_pairs.answer: A court may grant specific performance as a remedy for breach of contract when the subject matter of the contract is unique and monetary damages would not be sufficient to compensate the injured party. Specific performance is an order that requires the promisor to fulfill their contractual obligations as agreed. For example, if Emily signs a contract to sell Charlotte a gold samovar, a Russian antique of great sentimental value, and then repudiates the contract, a court may order Emily to perform her obligation and deliver the samovar to Charlotte. However, specific performance is not available for all types of contracts. It is typically limited to situations where the subject matter is unique, such as real estate or rare items. Additionally, specific performance is only granted at the discretion of the court and may not be issued if the contract involves personal services or if enforcing the order would be impractical or impossible.

If the claimant has given the other party a sum of money, there can be no dispute over the amount of the 
restitution interest. Tom gives Tim $100 to chop his tree into firewood. Tim repudiates. Tom’s restitution 
interest is $100. But serious difficulties can arise when the benefit conferred was performance. The courts 
have considerable discretion to award either the cost of hiring someone else to do the work that the 
injured party performed (generally, the market price of the service) or the value that was added to the 
property of the party in breach by virtue of the claimant’s performance. Mellors, a gardener, agrees to 
construct ten fences around Lady Chatterley’s flower gardens at the market price of $2,500. After erecting 
three, Mellors has performed services that would cost $750, market value. Assume that he has increased 
the value of the Lady’s grounds by $800. If the contract is repudiated, there are two measures of Mellors’s 
restitution interest: $800, the value by which the property was enhanced; or $750, the amount it would 
have cost Lady Chatterley to hire someone else to do the work. Which measure to use depends on who 
repudiated the contract and for what reason. 
 
Tort vs. Contract Remedies 
Frequently a contract breach may also amount to tortious conduct. A physician warrants her treatment as 
perfectly safe but performs the operation negligently, scarring the patient for life. The patient could sue 
for malpractice (tort) or for breach of warranty (contract). The choice involves at least four 
considerations: 
1. Statute of limitations. Most statutes of limitations prescribe longer periods for contract than for tort 
actions. 
2. Allowable damages. Punitive damages are more often permitted in tort actions, and certain kinds of 
injuries are compensable in tort but not in contract suits—for example, pain and suffering. 
3. Expert testimony. In most cases, the use of experts would be the same in either tort or contract suits, 
but in certain contract cases, the expert witness could be dispensed with, as, for example, in a contract 
case charging that the physician abandoned the patient. 
4. Insurance coverage. Most policies do not cover intentional torts, so a contract theory that avoids the 
element of willfulness would provide the plaintiff with a surer chance of recovering money damages.

an intention corresponding to the reasonable meaning of his words and acts.” 
 
At no time prior to the execution of the contract had Zehmer indicated to Lucy by word or act that he was 
not in earnest about selling the farm. They had argued about it and discussed its terms, as Zehmer 
admitted, for a long time. Lucy testified that if there was any jesting it was about paying $50,000 that 
night. The contract and the evidence show that he was not expected to pay the money that night. Zehmer 
said that after the writing was signed he laid it down on the counter in front of Lucy. Lucy said Zehmer 
handed it to him. In any event there had been what appeared to be a good faith offer and a good faith 
acceptance, followed by the execution and apparent delivery of a written contract. Both said that Lucy put 
the writing in his pocket and then offered Zehmer $5 to seal the bargain. Not until then, even under the 
defendants’ evidence, was anything said or done to indicate that the matter was a joke. Both of the 
Zehmers testified that when Zehmer asked his wife to sign he whispered that it was a joke so Lucy 
wouldn’t hear and that it was not intended that he should hear. 
 
The mental assent of the parties is not requisite for the formation of a contract. If the words or other acts 
of one of the parties have but one reasonable meaning, his undisclosed intention is immaterial except 
when an unreasonable meaning which he attaches to his manifestations is known to the other party.

Summary 
In this chapter we have seen that two fundamental sources of contract law are the common law as 
developed in the state courts and as summarized in the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, and the 
Uniform Commercial Code for the sale of goods. 
 
Sales law is a special type of contract law, governed by Article 2 of the UCC. Article 2 governs the sale of 
goods only, defined as things movable at the time of identification to the contract for sale. When the goods 
are “sold” incidental to a service, the courts do not agree on whether Article 2 applies. For two categories 
of goods, legislation specifically answers the question: foodstuffs served by a restaurant are goods; blood 
supplied for transfusions is not.

contracts implied by law; (2) bilateral and unilateral; (3) enforceable and unenforceable; and (4) 
completed (executed) and uncompleted (executory). To understand contract law, it is necessary to master 
these distinctions and their nuances.

qa_pairs.question: What are the four main distinctions in contract law that must be understood to determine the existence of a valid, enforceable contract?
qa_pairs.answer: The four main distinctions in contract law that are crucial for determining the existence of a valid, enforceable contract are: (1) contracts implied by law, which are those that the law assumes exist even though they are not explicitly stated; (2) bilateral contracts, where both parties make a promise to each other; and unilateral contracts, where only one party makes a promise in exchange for an act by the other party; (3) enforceable contracts, which are legally binding and can be upheld in a court of law, and unenforceable contracts, which cannot be enforced due to various reasons such as lack of consideration, illegality, or incapacity; and (4) completed contracts, which are fully executed and have been fulfilled by all parties, and uncompleted contracts, which are still in the process of being executed and have not yet been fully performed by all parties.

qa_pairs.question: What are the five questions that must be answered to determine whether a valid, enforceable contract exists?
qa_pairs.answer: To determine whether a valid, enforceable contract exists, the following five questions must be answered: (1) Did the parties reach an agreement, indicating that there was a mutual understanding and consent to the terms of the contract? (2) Was consideration present, meaning that something of value was exchanged between the parties, which is a necessary element for a contract to be valid? (3) Was the agreement legal, ensuring that the contract's subject matter and purpose do not violate any laws or public policies? (4) Did the parties have capacity to make a contract, which means that they were of legal age, sound mind, and not under duress or undue influence at the time of entering into the contract? (5) Was the agreement in the proper form, which refers to the requirements for a contract to be valid, such as being in writing if required by law or meeting the formalities of a specific type of contract, like a real estate contract.

Let’s analyze this sequence of events in legal terms—recognizing, of course, that this example is an 
analogy and that the law, even today, would not impose consequences on Alden for his failure to carry out 
Captain Standish’s wishes. Alden was the captain’s agent: he was specifically authorized to speak in his 
name in a manner agreed on, toward a specified end, and he accepted the assignment in consideration of 
the captain’s friendship. He had, however, a conflict of interest. He attempted to carry out the assignment, 
but he did not perform according to expectations. Eventually, he wound up with the prize himself. Here

that he had ridden at breakneck speed to reach Priscilla’s side and while en route ran into and 
injured a pedestrian on the road. Could the pedestrian have sued Standish? 
• 
Suppose Alden had injured himself on the journey. Would Standish be liable to Alden? 
•

qa_pairs.question: What was the nature of John Alden's authority as Captain Standish's agent, and how did it affect his actions towards Priscilla?
qa_pairs.answer: John Alden's authority as Captain Standish's agent was to speak on Standish's behalf, particularly in matters concerning the settlement and relations with the Native Americans. This authority was specific and limited to the tasks assigned by Standish. His failure to adhere to the agreed-upon mission and his personal involvement with Priscilla led to a significant conflict, culminating in the famous line, 'Why don’t you speak for yourself, John?' qa_pairs.question: In the context of agency law, what are the potential legal implications if John Alden had committed a tortious act while performing his duties as an agent for Captain Standish?
qa_pairs.answer: If John Alden had committed a tortious act while performing his duties as an agent for Captain Standish, the legal implications would depend on the nature of the tort and the relationship between the parties involved. Agency law typically holds the principal liable for the torts committed by the agent within the scope of their authority. If Alden's actions were within the scope of his authority and were intended to benefit Standish, Standish could potentially be held liable for any resulting harm. For example, if Alden had injured a pedestrian while rushing to Priscilla's side, the pedestrian could have sued Standish for damages. However, if Alden's actions were outside the scope of his authority or were motivated by personal interests, Standish might not be held liable. Additionally, if Alden had injured himself during the journey, Standish's liability would depend on whether the injury was a foreseeable consequence of the agency relationship. The principal-agent relationship is complex, and the determination of liability often requires a careful analysis of the agent's authority, the nature of the tort, and the intentions behind the agent's actions.

Types of Agents 
There are five types of agents. 
 
 
General Agent 
The general agent possesses the authority to carry out a broad range of transactions in the name and on 
behalf of the principal. The general agent may be the manager of a business or may have a more limited 
but nevertheless ongoing role—for example, as a purchasing agent or as a life insurance agent authorized 
to sign up customers for the home office. In either case, the general agent has authority to alter the 
principal’s legal relationships with third parties. One who is designated a general agent has the authority

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a general agent and a special agent in terms of their authority to act on behalf of the principal?
qa_pairs.answer: A general agent possesses the authority to carry out a broad range of transactions in the name and on behalf of the principal, whereas a special agent is limited to acting only in a specifically designated instance or in a specifically designated set of transactions. For example, a general agent might be a business manager with ongoing responsibilities, such as a purchasing agent or a life insurance agent authorized to sign up customers for the home office. In contrast, a special agent, like a real estate broker, is hired for a specific purpose, such as finding a buyer for the principal's land. The general agent's authority is broad and ongoing, while the special agent's authority is limited to specific tasks or transactions.

qa_pairs.question: Can a principal limit the authority of a general agent, and if so, how?
qa_pairs.answer: Yes, a principal can limit the authority of a general agent by explicitly spelling out the limitations. However, even with these limitations, the principal may still be liable for any actions taken by the agent that exceed the agent's authority. To restrict the general agent's authority, the principal must clearly define the boundaries of the agent's powers. This can be done through a written agreement or contract that specifies the scope of the agent's authority and any restrictions. For instance, if a general agent is authorized to manage a business but not to enter into certain types of contracts, this should be clearly stated in the agreement. By doing so, the principal can protect themselves from potential liabilities arising from the agent's actions outside of their authorized scope.

Servant 
The final category of agent is the servant. Until the early nineteenth century, any employee whose work 
duties were subject to an employer’s control was called a servant; we would not use that term so broadly 
in modern English. The Restatement (Second) of Agency, Section 2, defines a servant as “an agent 
employed by a master [employer] to perform service in his affairs whose physical conduct in the 
performance of the service is controlled or is subject to the right to control by the master.” 
 
Independent Contractor 
Not every contract for services necessarily creates a master-servant relationship. There is an important 
distinction made between the status of a servant and that of an independent contractor. According to 
the Restatement (Second) of Agency, Section 2, “an independent contractor is a person who contracts 
with another to do something for him but who is not controlled by the other nor subject to the other’s 
right to control with respect to his physical conduct in the performance of the undertaking.” As the name 
implies, the independent contractor is legally autonomous. A plumber salaried to a building contractor is 
an employee and agent of the contractor. But a plumber who hires himself out to repair pipes in people’s 
homes is an independent contractor. If you hire a lawyer to settle a dispute, that person is not your 
employee or your servant; she is an independent contractor. The terms “agent” and “independent

qa_pairs.question: What is the legal distinction between a servant and an independent contractor according to the Restatement (Second) of Agency, Section 2?
qa_pairs.answer: The Restatement (Second) of Agency, Section 2, defines a servant as an agent employed by a master (employer) to perform service in his affairs, whose physical conduct in the performance of the service is controlled or subject to the right to control by the master. In contrast, an independent contractor is a person who contracts with another to do something for him but is not controlled by the other nor subject to the other’s right to control with respect to his physical conduct in the performance of the undertaking. This distinction is crucial as it determines the legal and financial responsibilities of the parties involved. For instance, employers are required to withhold income taxes from their employees' paychecks, but payments to independent contractors, such as plumbers, do not require such withholding. The line between a servant and an independent contractor is not always clearly drawn, but generally, a servant is under the employer's control, while an independent contractor operates autonomously.

qa_pairs.question: Why is the distinction between an agent and an independent contractor important for taxation, workers' compensation, and liability insurance?
qa_pairs.answer: The distinction between an agent and an independent contractor is significant for several legal and financial reasons. For taxation purposes, employers are mandated to withhold income taxes from their employees' paychecks, a requirement that does not apply to payments made to independent contractors. This distinction affects how income is reported and taxed. In terms of workers' compensation, employees (servants) are typically covered under their employer's workers' compensation insurance, providing benefits in case of work-related injuries. Independent contractors, however, are not covered under such insurance, which means they must arrange their own coverage. Lastly, liability insurance implications differ as well; employers may be held liable for the actions of their employees, whereas liability for independent contractors' actions generally falls on the contractor themselves. These distinctions help clarify the responsibilities and protections afforded to each party in a contractual relationship.

qa_pairs.question: How can an agency relationship be created according to the text, and what are the three contract principles that are especially important for agencies created by agreement?
qa_pairs.answer: An agency relationship can be created in two ways: by agreement (expressly) or by operation of law (constructively or impliedly). When agencies are created by agreement, they are often governed by the general rules of contract law, which include three important principles: the requirement for consideration, the necessity for a writing, and concerns regarding contractual capacity. Consideration is a fundamental element of a contract, meaning that there must be something of value exchanged between the parties. A writing refers to the requirement that certain agreements must be in writing to be enforceable. Contractual capacity concerns the ability of the parties to enter into a contract, which typically means they must be of legal age and sound mind. These principles ensure that the agency relationship is legally binding and enforceable.

Agency Created by Operation of Law 
Most agencies are made by contract, but agency also may arise impliedly or apparently. 
 
Implied Agency 
In areas of social need, courts have declared an agency to exist in the absence of an agreement. The agency 
relationship then is said to have been implied “by operation of law.” Children in most states may purchase 
necessary items—food or medical services—on the parent’s account. Long-standing social policy deems it 
desirable for the head of a family to support his dependents, and the courts will put the expense on the 
family head in order to provide for the dependents’ welfare. The courts achieve this result by supposing 
the dependent to be the family head’s agent, thus allowing creditors to sue the family head for the debt. 
 
Implied agencies also arise where one person behaves as an agent would and the “principal,” knowing that 
the “agent” is behaving so, acquiesces, allowing the person to hold himself out as an agent. Such are the 
basic facts in Weingart v. Directoire Restaurant, Inc. in Section 9.3.1 "Creation of Agency: Liability of 
Parent for Contracts Made by “Agent” Child". 
 
Apparent Agency 
Suppose Arthur is Paul’s agent, employed through October 31. On November 1, Arthur buys materials at 
Lumber Yard—as he has been doing since early spring—and charges them to Paul’s account. Lumber Yard, 
not knowing that Arthur’s employment terminated the day before, bills Paul. Will Paul have to pay? Yes, 
because the termination of the agency was not communicated to Lumber Yard. It appeared that Arthur 
was an authorized agent. This issue is discussed further in Chapter 10 "Liability of Principal and Agent; 
Termination of Agency".

qa_pairs.question: What are the different ways an agency relationship can be created according to the text?
qa_pairs.answer: An agency relationship can be created in several ways as outlined in the text. Firstly, it can be created expressly through a contract between the principal and the agent. This is the most common method where both parties agree on the terms of the agency relationship. Secondly, an agency relationship can arise impliedly or apparently without a formal agreement. Implied agency occurs in situations where the law infers an agency relationship due to social needs or long-standing practices, such as a parent purchasing necessary items for their children or a family head being held liable for debts incurred by the family. Apparent agency, on the other hand, arises when a person behaves as an agent and the principal, aware of this behavior, allows the person to act as an agent. This can lead to situations where the principal may be held liable for the actions of the person acting as an agent, even if there was no formal agreement. The text also mentions that agencies can be created by operation of law, where the courts may declare an agency relationship to exist in the absence of an agreement to fulfill social policies or protect the interests of dependents.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances can a mentally incompetent agent bind a principal, and what are the implications of such a situation?
qa_pairs.answer: A mentally incompetent agent cannot bind a principal because the capacity of the agent is crucial for the formation of a valid agency relationship. The text explains that for an agency to be legally binding, both the principal and the agent must have the capacity to enter into a contract. If an agent is mentally incompetent, they lack the necessary capacity to act on behalf of the principal, and therefore, any contract or agreement made by such an agent would not be enforceable against the principal. The implications of this situation are significant, as it protects the principal from being held liable for the actions or agreements made by an agent who is not legally capable of acting. This ensures that the principal's interests are safeguarded and that they are not bound by the actions of an agent who may not have the ability to understand or fulfill the terms of the agency relationship.

qa_pairs.question: Why is agency law especially important in the business and government context?
qa_pairs.answer: Agency law is particularly crucial in the business and government sectors because corporations, which are legal entities, cannot act on their own. Instead, they operate through agents who act on their behalf. This creates a complex web of relationships and responsibilities that must be clearly defined and regulated. In the business context, agency law helps to establish the scope of an agent's authority, ensuring that agents act within the limits of their powers and in the best interests of the principal. It also clarifies the duties and obligations between the agent and the principal, which is essential for maintaining trust and accountability. In the government context, agency law is vital for the creation and operation of governmental agencies, which may be established expressly, impliedly, or apparently. It ensures that these agencies function effectively and in accordance with the law, and it helps to resolve recurring issues such as the true nature of the agent, the extent of the agent's authority, and the duties among the parties involved. Overall, agency law provides a framework for managing the relationships between principals and agents, which is fundamental to the smooth operation of both business and government entities.

qa_pairs.question: What are the five types of agents?
qa_pairs.answer: The five types of agents in agency law are: general agent, special agent, subagent, agency coupled with an interest, and servant (or employee). A general agent has broad authority to act on behalf of the principal in a wide range of matters, while a special agent is limited to specific tasks or transactions. A subagent is appointed by an agent to perform duties on behalf of the principal, often when the agent is unable to do so. An agency coupled with an interest is a unique type of agency where the agent has a personal interest in the subject matter of the agency, which provides the agent with a right to the subject matter that cannot be revoked by the principal. Lastly, a servant or employee is an agent who is employed by the principal to perform services, and this relationship is typically characterized by a lack of independence compared to other types of agents. Each type of agent has distinct characteristics and implications for the duties and responsibilities of the parties involved.

Duty to Avoid Self-Dealing 
A fiduciary may not lawfully profit from a conflict between his personal interest in a transaction and his 
principal’s interest in that same transaction. A broker hired as a purchasing agent, for instance, may not 
sell to his principal through a company in which he or his family has a financial interest. The penalty for 
breach of fiduciary duty is loss of compensation and profit and possible damages for breach of trust.

qa_pairs.answer: The fiduciary duty imposed on an agent by law requires the agent to subordinate his self-interest to that of his principal. This duty goes beyond the terms of the contract and is not limited to merely abiding by the contract terms. qa_pairs.question: What are the consequences of a breach of fiduciary duty by an agent, and what specific duties does it involve?
qa_pairs.answer: The consequences of a breach of fiduciary duty by an agent can include loss of compensation and profit, as well as possible damages for breach of trust. The specific duties involved in a breach of fiduciary duty include the duty to avoid self-dealing and the duty to preserve confidential information. The duty to avoid self-dealing prohibits an agent from lawfully profiting from a conflict between his personal interest in a transaction and his principal’s interest in that same transaction. For example, a broker hired as a purchasing agent may not sell to his principal through a company in which he or his family has a financial interest. The duty to preserve confidential information requires an agent to protect information confidentially given or acquired by the principal, such as how much the principal is willing to sell or pay for property, marketing strategies, and other sensitive information. The law prohibits an agent from using this information for his own purposes or in ways that would injure the interests of the principal, even if the information is gleaned from the principal through unrelated means.

Other Duties 
In addition to fiduciary responsibility (and whatever special duties may be contained in the specific 
contract) the law of agency imposes other duties on an agent. These duties are not necessarily unique to 
agents: a nonfiduciary employee could also be bound to these duties on the right facts. 
 
Duty of Skill and Care 
An agent is usually taken on because he has special knowledge or skills that the principal wishes to tap. 
The agent is under a legal duty to perform his work with the care and skill that is “standard in the locality 
for the kind of work which he is employed to perform” and to exercise any special skills, if these are 
greater or more refined than those prevalent among those normally employed in the community. In short, 
the agent may not lawfully do a sloppy job. [2]

qa_pairs.question: What is the legal duty of an agent regarding the use of confidential information obtained during their agency?
qa_pairs.answer: An agent is legally bound not to use confidential information obtained during their agency for the principal's benefit after their agency has ended. This includes information such as trade secrets and customer lists. Even if the agent is free to compete with the principal after resigning, they cannot use the confidential information they acquired while acting on behalf of the principal. This duty of confidentiality is a fiduciary responsibility, and breaching it can lead to legal consequences. The case of Bacon v. Volvo Service Center, Inc. specifically addresses the breach of this duty of confidentiality.

qa_pairs.question: What are the duties of an agent that are not necessarily unique to agents but could apply to nonfiduciary employees under certain circumstances?
qa_pairs.answer: In addition to the fiduciary responsibilities and any special duties outlined in the specific contract, an agent is also subject to other duties that are not unique to agents but could apply to nonfiduciary employees under certain circumstances. These duties include the duty of skill and care, where the agent must perform their work with the care and skill that is standard in the locality for the kind of work they are employed to perform, and the duty of good conduct, which requires the agent to act in a manner that does not bring disrepute to the business. The agent must also keep accurate financial records and act only as authorized by the principal. These duties ensure that the agent conducts themselves in a professional and responsible manner, maintaining the integrity and reputation of the business.

This duty states a truism but is one for which there are limits. A principal’s wishes may have been stated 
ambiguously or may be broad enough to confer discretion on the agent. As long as the agent acts 
reasonably under the circumstances, he will not be liable for damages later if the principal ultimately 
repudiates what the agent has done: “Only conduct which is contrary to the principal’s manifestations to 
him, interpreted in light of what he has reason to know at the time when he acts,…subjects the agent to 
liability to the principal.”[3] 
 
Duty Not to Attempt the Impossible or Impracticable 
The principal says to the agent, “Keep working until the job is done.” The agent is not obligated to go 
without food or sleep because the principal misapprehended how long it would take to complete the job. 
Nor should the agent continue to expend the principal’s funds in a quixotic attempt to gain business, sign 
up customers, or produce inventory when it is reasonably clear that such efforts would be in vain.

patent to him. A third employee invented a safety device and also assigned the patent to Sharp. At one 
time, Sharp’s son invented a leakproof bolt and a process to manufacture it; these, too, were assigned to 
Sharp. These inventions were developed in the company’s plants at its expense.

In the case of Grip Nut Co. v. Sharp, the court applied this doctrine when Sharp, who had assigned his inventions to the company, continued to work for the company after his employment contract expired. After Sharp's death, his family claimed the rights to these inventions and sued the company for patent infringement. The court disagreed with the family's claim, invoking the 'Shop Rights' Doctrine. The court ruled that since the inventions were developed and perfected in the company's plant with its resources and at its expense, the company had the right to use them without paying royalties to Sharp's estate.

qa_pairs.question: What is the duty of an agent to inform the principal and what are the potential consequences of failing to do so?
qa_pairs.answer: An agent has a duty to inform the principal of any information that is relevant to matters entrusted to him. This duty is particularly critical because information in the hands of an agent is generally imputed to the principal, whose legal liabilities to third parties may depend on receiving this information in a timely manner. For instance, service of process requires a defendant to respond within a certain number of days, and an agent's failure to communicate to the principal that a summons has been served may prevent the principal from defending a lawsuit. The imputation of knowledge to the principal is strict, meaning that even if the agent is acting against the principal's interests, a third party may still rely on the agent's notification unless the third party knows the agent is acting adversely. Therefore, an agent's failure to fulfill this duty can have serious legal consequences for the principal.

Principal’s Duty to Agent 
In this category, we may note that the principal owes the agent duties in contract, tort, and—statutorily—
workers’ compensation law. 
 
Contract Duties 
The fiduciary relationship of agent to principal does not run in reverse—that is, the principal is not the 
agent’s fiduciary. Nevertheless, the principal has a number of contractually related obligations toward his 
agent. 
 
General Contract Duties 
These duties are analogues of many of the agent’s duties that we have just examined. In brief, a principal 
has a duty “to refrain from unreasonably interfering with [an agent’s] work.” [5] The principal is allowed, 
however, to compete with the agent unless the agreement specifically prohibits it. The principal has a duty 
to inform his agent of risks of physical harm or pecuniary loss that inhere in the agent’s performance of 
assigned tasks. Failure to warn an agent that travel in a particular neighborhood required by the job may 
be dangerous (a fact unknown to the agent but known to the principal) could under common law subject 
the principal to a suit for damages if the agent is injured while in the neighborhood performing her job. A

and the customs of the particular business. An agent’s reputation is no less valuable than a principal’s, 
and so an agent is under no obligation to continue working for one who sullies it.

qa_pairs.question: What are the contract duties that a principal owes to an agent, and how do they relate to the agent's duties?
qa_pairs.answer: A principal owes several contractually related obligations to an agent, despite the fact that the fiduciary relationship of agent to principal does not run in reverse. These duties include the principal's duty to refrain from unreasonably interfering with the agent's work, the duty to inform the agent of risks of physical harm or pecuniary loss that may arise from assigned tasks, and the obligation to render accounts of monies due to the agent. The principal's duty to inform the agent of risks is particularly important, as failure to warn an agent about known dangers, such as the need to travel in a dangerous neighborhood for work, could subject the principal to a suit for damages if the agent is injured. Additionally, the principal is obliged to render accounts of monies due to the agent, with the extent of this obligation depending on factors such as the agent's independence, the method of compensation, and the customs of the particular business. The principal's obligation to render accounts is analogous to the agent's duty to account to the principal. Furthermore, an agent's reputation is valuable, and a principal is under no obligation to continue working with an agent who sullies it. These contract duties of the principal are analogues of many of the agent's duties, reflecting the reciprocal nature of the agent-principal relationship.

Employment at Will 
Under the traditional “employment-at-will” doctrine, an employee who is not hired for a specific period 
can be fired at any time, for any reason (except bad reasons: an employee cannot be fired, for example, for 
reporting that his employer’s paper mill is illegally polluting groundwater). This doctrine has been much 
criticized. 
 
Duty to Indemnify 
Agents commonly spend money pursuing the principal’s business. Unless the agreement explicitly 
provides otherwise, the principal has a duty to indemnify or reimburse the agent. A familiar form of 
indemnity is the employee expense account. 
 
Tort and Workers’ Compensation Duties 
The employer owes the employee—any employee, not just agents—certain statutorily imposed tort and 
workers’ compensation duties. 
 
Background to Workers’ Compensation 
Andy, who works in a dynamite factory, negligently stores dynamite in the wrong shed. Andy warns his 
fellow employee Bill that he has done so. Bill lights up a cigarette near the shed anyway, a spark lands on 
the ground, the dynamite explodes, and Bill is injured. May Bill sue his employer to recover damages? At 
common law, the answer would be no—three times no. First, the “fellow-servant” rule would bar recovery 
because the employer was held not to be responsible for torts committed by one employee against 
another. Second, Bill’s failure to heed Andy’s warning and his decision to smoke near the dynamite 
amounted to contributory negligence. Hence even if the dynamite had been negligently stored by the 
employer rather than by a fellow employee, the claim would have been dismissed. Third, the courts might
